Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels mediate insect thermosensation, yet the downstream neurotransmitter pathways linking TRP activation to behavioral output remain unclear. We investigated the role of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) in thermoregulatory and neural responses induced by TRP ligands in the American cockroach, Periplaneta americana. Extracellular recordings from the ventral nerve cord showed that capsaicin reduced spontaneous neuronal firing, whereas the selective α7-containing nAChR antagonist MG 624 increased baseline activity. Notably, nicotinic receptor blockade prevented the capsaicin-induced suppression of neuronal activity, suggesting an interaction between cholinergic signaling and capsaicin-induced neuronal modulation. Behaviorally, capsaicin shifted thermal preference toward cooler temperatures, consistent with TRP-mediated heat avoidance. This response, as well as the effect of the TRPV1 antagonist capsazepine, was markedly attenuated by MG 624 pretreatment. Grooming assays revealed differential modulation of antennal and leg grooming, suggesting distinct neural mechanisms and partial interaction between cholinergic and monoaminergic pathways. Despite pronounced neural and behavioral effects, neither TRP ligands nor nicotinic receptor blockade significantly altered whole-animal metabolic rate, as assessed by CO₂ production. Together, these findings indicate that cholinergic signaling contributes to behavioral responses induced by TRP ligands and interacts with capsaicin-induced neuronal modulation in P. americana. The results provide new insight into the neurochemical integration of thermosensory signaling and highlight cholinergic pathways as important contributors to insect thermoregulatory responses.

Introduction

Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels comprise a diverse superfamily of polymodal cation channels that mediate the detection and integration of environmental stimuli across animal taxa. In insects, TRP channels participate in thermosensation, chemosensation, osmosensation, and mechanosensation, thereby contributing to the maintenance of physiological homeostasis and adaptive behavior. Notably, several insect TRP channels exhibit dual functionality, operating both as thermosensors and chemoreceptors. The TRPA channel Painless, first characterized in Drosophila melanogaster, was among the earliest identified insect TRP channels implicated in avoidance of noxious heat (Tracey et al. 2003). Expressed in both central and peripheral components of the nervous system, Painless functions as a high-threshold heat receptor activated by temperatures exceeding 42 °C (Sokabe and Tominaga 2009; Dillon et al. 2009; McKemy 2007). To date, at least twelve TRP family members have been associated with thermosensory processes in insects (Rosenzweig et al. 2008; Kwon et al. 2010; Kohno et al. 2010; Gallio et al. 2011; Turner et al. 2016).

Beyond thermal activation, insect TRP channels respond to a broad spectrum of chemical ligands. Allyl isothiocyanate (AITC), a plant-derived electrophile, activates insect heat-sensitive TRP channels (Mendel et al. 2018). Menthol modulates the activity of TRPM and TRPA channels in D. melanogaster (Himmel et al. 2019), while capsaicin has been shown to activate Painless in this species (Li et al. 2020). In addition, our previous studies indicate that capsaicin may act as a functional ligand of TRP thermoreceptors in the American cockroach, Periplaneta americana (Maliszewska et al. 2018), suggesting evolutionary conservation of chemosensory–thermosensory integration.

Although numerous studies have described behavioral and physiological responses associated with TRP channel activation in insects, considerably less is known about the neural mechanisms that connect TRP-mediated sensory detection with downstream neurochemical signaling. Our recent findings in P. americana demonstrated that pharmacological activation of TRP channels increases octopamine levels (Maliszewska et al. 2024), indicating that TRP-dependent sensory signaling engages broader neuromodulatory networks. Because TRP channels, including Painless, are Ca²⁺-permeable and mediate rapid calcium influx upon activation (Sokabe et al. 2008), stimulation of thermosensory afferents is expected to trigger neurotransmitter release. The increase in octopamine observed following TRP activation suggests that sensory signals originating from TRP-expressing neurons are transmitted through excitatory pathways to downstream octopaminergic circuits. Given that acetylcholine (ACh) is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the insect nervous system, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors represents plausible candidates for mediating the transfer of TRP-dependent sensory information to neural networks involved in thermoregulation and behavior.

Therefore, we hypothesize that acetylcholine may participate in the transmission of thermosensory signals generated by TRP channel activation. In D. melanogaster, thermal information detected by peripheral sensory neurons is projected to the ventroposterior glomeruli of the antennal lobe, where further processing occurs (Marin et al. 2020). Similar central processing of thermal information has been demonstrated in the cockroach Periplaneta americana. Anatomical studies have shown that antennal cold receptor neurons project to specific regions of the deutocerebrum, providing direct sensory input to central thermosensory pathways (Nishikawa et al. 1995), while electrophysiological recordings have identified deutocerebral interneurons that respond to temperature changes detected by the antennae (Nishikawa et al. 1991). Together, these findings demonstrate that thermal cues are processed by dedicated central neural circuits. Evidence from recent molecular and functional studies in Drosophila further suggest that cholinergic signaling is involved in this pathway, as thermosensory neuron populations express cholinergic markers and form excitatory connections within central thermosensory circuits (Jin et al. 2021; Li et al. 2022; Corthals et al. 2023; Alpert et al. 2020). Collectively, these observations support the view that acetylcholine contributes to the central processing and integration of thermal information. The insect cholinergic system shares key organizational and molecular features with that of vertebrates, comprising choline acetyltransferase, acetylcholinesterases, high-affinity choline transporters, and two major receptor classes: ionotropic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) and metabotropic muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChRs) (Grünewald and Siefert 2019).

Insect nAChRs are pentameric ligand-gated ion channels that mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are essential for locomotion, learning, and memory (Thany 2025). Multiple receptor subtypes have been identified in the insect CNS, including pharmacologically distinct α-bungarotoxin-sensitive and α-bungarotoxin-insensitive classes. Homomeric receptors containing α7-like subunits display sensitivity to α-bungarotoxin, analogous to vertebrate α7 nAChRs. In P. americana, nAChRs with distinct pharmacological profiles have been described in dorsal unpaired median (DUM) neurons, Df motor neurons, and thoracic ganglia (Thany et al. 2007; Salgado 2021), underscoring the functional heterogeneity of cholinergic transmission in this species.

Despite the well-established role of cholinergic transmission in insect neural function, its contribution to thermoregulation and thermosensory integration remains poorly understood. In the honeybee, Apis mellifera, activation of nAChRs has been shown to alter thoracic temperature (Tosi et al. 2016), indicating a functional link between cholinergic signaling and thermal physiology. Furthermore, interactions between ACh and defined neuronal populations, such as those expressing the Allatostatin-C receptor AstC-R2, may coordinate physiological adaptations to thermal stress, including diapause and reproductive dormancy under low-temperature conditions (Meiselman et al. 2022).

The present study investigates whether thermoregulatory behavioral changes induced by TRP ligands, particularly capsaicin, are mediated via cholinergic mechanisms in P. americana, with specific emphasis on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. By elucidating the functional interplay between TRP channels and cholinergic signaling pathways, we aim to clarify the neurochemical mechanisms underlying insect thermosensation and adaptive responses to thermal stress, contributing to a comparative understanding of sensory integration in ectothermic animals.

Materials and methods

Insects

Experiments were performed on adult males of the American cockroach, Periplaneta americana L. Individuals originated from a laboratory colony maintained at Nicolaus Copernicus University (Toruń, Poland). Insects were housed in plastic containers under controlled environmental conditions (28 ± 2 °C; 12:12 h light: dark photoperiod) with ad libitum access to water and standard diet.

Tested substances

Capsaicin (cat. no. M2028; Merck Life Science, Darmstadt, Germany) was initially dissolved in ethanol and subsequently diluted in physiological saline to a final concentration of 1 µM. The final ethanol concentration in all working solutions was 0.01%; the same vehicle solution served as control. Capsazepine (cat. no. C191; Merck Life Science, Darmstadt, Germany) was prepared analogously. MG 624 (cat. no. 1356; Tocris Bioscience, Bristol, UK), a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist, was likewise dissolved in ethanol and diluted in saline to 1 µM. Compounds were applied topically in a volume of 10 µL to the dorsal thorax.

Electrophysiological recordings

Extracellular electrophysiological recordings were made on semi-isolated nerve cord of Periplaneta americana. Adult male cockroaches were deprived of head, legs and wings and were mounted ventral side down to the cork stand. Using microscissors, the cuticle, digestive system and accessory gland were removed to exhibit the nerve cord. Preparation was kept wet using physiological saline (in mM: NaCl—210, KCl—3.1, CaCl2—5, MgCl2—5.4, Hepes—5; pH = 7.4 was adjusted with NaOH). Spiker box system (Backyard Brains, An Arbor, MI USA) (Marzullo et al. 2012) was used for recording. Two electrodes were placed in the vicinity of abdominal part of nerve cord and the signal was processed by a differential amplifier. Data was registered using dedicated software SpikeRecorder. The recording was started when the nerve activity remained stable for 3 min., then 5 min. of control pre-treatment recording was performed. The average frequency of pre-treatment recordings was set as 1 for further calculations. In each experiment the tested substance was applied in 20 µL volume and recording was continued for at least next 20 min. Data was then processed in SpikeRecorder software, the frequency of spontaneous extracellular action potential was analyzed, then normalized to pre-treatment recordings.

Thermal preferences assay

Thermal preference was assessed using a linear temperature gradient apparatus as previously described (Maliszewska et al. 2018). The system consisted of an aluminum trough (60 × 4 × 2 cm). One end was connected to a thermostat (Polyscience 8006A12E) circulating warm water, while the opposite end was connected to a cryostat (Polyscience 9106AA2E) supplying cold water, generating a stable gradient ranging from 10 °C to 40 °C. The trough was divided into 20 equal compartments (3 cm each). Temperatures were verified before each trial using a digital thermometer (UT321, Sinometer Instruments).

Immediately following topical treatment, insects were placed in the central compartment (~ 24 °C). For combined treatments, MG 624 was administered 30 min prior to capsaicin or capsazepine application. Each assay involved a single insect per gradient apparatus. Individuals remained in the gradient for 24 h. Behavioral activity was recorded using digital video cameras (SONY HDR-XR200VE or SONY FDR-AX33) and BioVid software (FERRO Software). Twenty-second video segments were captured every 160 s. Insect position within the gradient was subsequently analyzed to determine preferred temperature over time.

Grooming behavior

Grooming was quantified during a 30-min observation period preceded by a 5-min habituation phase. Individual cockroaches were transferred to glass observation chambers immediately after topical treatment with capsaicin (1 µM, 10 µL), MG-624 (1 µM, 10 µL), or vehicle (0.01% ethanol in saline, 10 µL). In pretreatment experiments, MG 624 was applied 15 min before capsaicin. Behavioral assays were conducted between 2 and 8 h after the onset of the light phase. Ambient temperature during testing was maintained at 23–25 °C. Time spent grooming the antennae and legs was measured manually using a stopwatch during the 30-min observation period.

Metabolic rate

Metabolic rate was estimated by measuring carbon dioxide production (V̇CO₂) using an infrared CO₂ analyzer (S157, Qubit Systems Inc., Kingston, Canada) calibrated with certified reference gas (500 ppm CO₂). The analyzer operated within a flow-through respirometry system. Compressed ambient air (21% O₂, 79% N₂) was drawn through 5 mL glass respirometry chambers using a pump (P652, Qubit Systems Inc.) at a constant flow rate of 150 mL min⁻¹. Water vapor was removed from the air stream using magnesium perchlorate.

Prior to measurements, insects were deprived of food for approximately 2 h to minimize postprandial metabolic effects. Each individual was weighed (Radwag WTB 200 analytical balance) immediately before testing. Following treatment, cockroaches were placed individually into chambers for a 2-h recording session. Baseline measurements (empty chamber) were taken for 3 min every 15 min to correct for system drift. All measurements were conducted at 25 ± 2 °C.

Data analysis

Electrophysiological data were analyzed using the Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Mann–Whitney U tests. Thermal preference data were analyzed using a two-way General Linear Model (GLM), with treatment as a fixed factor and time (24 h divided into 2-h intervals) as a repeated-measures factor. Post hoc comparisons were conducted using the Least Significant Difference (LSD) test. Grooming data were log-transformed to meet assumptions of normality and analyzed by one-way ANOVA followed by LSD post hoc tests. Carbon dioxide production was analyzed using ANCOVA, with body mass included as a covariate. All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 25 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Differences were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05.

Results

Nicotinic receptor blockade attenuates the electrophysiological response to capsaicin

Direct application of capsaicin produced a marked suppression of spontaneous extracellular activity in the abdominal nerve cord of Periplaneta americana. Mean spike frequency decreased by approximately 45% relative to baseline values (p < 0.001; Fig. 1).

In contrast, treatment with the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist MG 624 alone significantly increased spontaneous neuronal firing. During MG 624 exposure, spike frequency reached 2.91-fold of control levels, indicating a pronounced elevation of baseline excitability (Fig. 1). These results suggest that nicotinic acetylcholine receptors contribute to the regulation of resting neuronal activity within the ventral nerve cord and that their blockade alters the balance of neuronal excitability in this network. When MG 624 was administered prior to capsaicin, the typical capsaicin-induced suppression of neuronal activity was abolished (p = 0.01). Under these conditions, spike frequency remained comparable to that observed following MG 624 alone, suggesting an interaction between the effects of MG 624 and capsaicin on spontaneous neuronal activity.

Behavioral responses to TRP ligands depend on intact nicotinic signaling

Consistent with electrophysiological findings, behavioral thermoregulation was significantly affected by pharmacological manipulations (GLM: F = 2.76; df = 2; p = 0.04). Capsaicin treatment induced a shift in thermal preference toward cooler regions of the gradient (Fig. 2). However, this effect was completely abolished by pretreatment with MG 624. In fact, insects receiving MG 624 prior to capsaicin selected significantly higher temperatures during the first 3 h of observation compared to the capsaicin-only group.

To determine whether this interaction was specific to capsaicin-induced TRP activation, we examined the effects of capsazepine (CPZ), a TRPV1 antagonist. Capsazepine alone induced preference for higher ambient temperatures. However, combined administration of MG 624 and capsazepine significantly attenuated this effect (GLM: F = 8.3; df = 2; p = 0.004). Cockroaches treated with both compounds selected cooler temperatures than those exposed to capsazepine alone (Fig. 3), indicating that nicotinic signaling contributes broadly to TRP-dependent thermoregulatory behavior. In the combined-treatment groups (MG 624 + CPS and MG 624 + CPZ), the values recorded at 0 min were obtained after MG 624 administration but before the application of capsaicin or capsazepine. Therefore, any differences observed at this time point cannot be attributed to the TRP ligands and most likely reflect natural inter-individual variability among the independently assigned groups.

Grooming behavior

Antennal grooming was not significantly altered by capsaicin alone (29.8 ± 7.8 s; 86% of control levels). In contrast, MG 624 markedly increased antennal grooming (106.6 ± 30.3 s), representing approximately a threefold increase over control values and 3.59-fold over the capsaicin group (p = 0.02; Fig. 4A).

Pretreatment with MG 624 prior to capsaicin did not significantly differ from capsaicin alone (p = 0.051), suggesting that nicotinic receptor blockade does not further enhance capsaicin-induced antennal grooming under these conditions.

Leg grooming was significantly elevated following both capsaicin (p = 0.04) and MG 624 (p = 0.009) administration compared to controls. Cockroaches pretreated with MG 624 and subsequently exposed to capsaicin spent 237.7 ± 48 s grooming their legs, corresponding to a 2.2-fold increase relative to controls (p = 0.006). However, no significant differences were detected between capsaicin alone, MG 624 alone, and the combined treatment (Fig. 4B).

Metabolic rate is not significantly affected by TRP or nicotinic stimulation

Given that both thermoregulatory shifts and grooming involve sustained motor activity, we examined whether these behavioral and electrophysiological effects were accompanied by changes in metabolic rate, as estimated by CO₂ production.

No statistically significant differences in mass-specific CO₂ production were observed among treatment groups. Mean CO₂ production in controls was 493.86 ± 66.11 µL h⁻¹ g⁻¹. Treated groups ranged from 381.56 ± 71.1 µL h⁻¹ g⁻¹ (MG 624 + CPS) to 560.95 ± 207.17 µL h⁻¹ g⁻¹ (MG 624 + CPZ). Although capsaicin alone (403.67 ± 34.33 µL h⁻¹ g⁻¹) and MG 624 + capsaicin (381.56 ± 71.1 µL h⁻¹ g⁻¹) showed numerically lower values than controls, and capsazepine-treated groups exhibited higher means, none of these differences reached statistical significance. Thus, neither TRP modulation nor nicotinic receptor blockade produced consistent or robust alterations in whole-animal metabolic rate under the present experimental conditions (Fig. 5).

Discussion

Thermosensation in insects relies on a distributed network of molecular sensors and neural circuits that integrate peripheral thermal input with central processing. Although the involvement of TRP channels in insect thermodetection is well established, considerably less is known about the downstream neurotransmitter systems that translate TRP activation into coordinated physiological and behavioral responses. In the present study, we investigated the contribution of the cholinergic system—specifically nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs)—to behavioral and electrophysiological effects induced by TRP ligands in the American cockroach, Periplaneta americana. Our findings provide evidence that nicotinic signaling constitutes an important component of TRP-dependent thermoregulatory responses.

To probe the involvement of nAChRs, we employed MG 624, a selective antagonist of neuronal α7-subunit–containing receptors (Gotti et al. 1998). Knowledge regarding the pharmacological properties of α7-like receptors in insects remains limited. Previous unpublished work from our laboratory demonstrated that MG 624 significantly reduced stimulus-evoked compound action potentials recorded from the connective exiting the terminal abdominal ganglion. In the cockroach escape circuit, such stimulus-evoked responses are brief and precisely timed, mediating rapid transmission of sensory information to trigger escape behavior. Comparable roles of α7-containing nAChRs have been described in other insects. In Drosophila melanogaster, α7 subunits contribute to visually mediated escape circuits (Fayyazuddin et al. 2006). A defining characteristic of α7 receptors is their rapid desensitization upon acetylcholine binding. This kinetic profile is consistent with our earlier observations that stimulus-evoked responses are short-lived and abruptly terminate, likely reflecting strong presynaptic acetylcholine release followed by rapid receptor inactivation. Such dynamics enable the generation of neural signals clearly distinguishable from spontaneous background activity. In the present experiments, administration of MG 624 induced a rapid increase in the frequency of spontaneous activity recorded from the ventral nerve cord. At first glance, this finding may appear unexpected, given that acetylcholine serves as the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the insect nervous system and antagonism of nAChRs would generally be predicted to reduce neural activity. However, the signals recorded from the abdominal connectives reflects the integrated output of a complex neural network that includes sensory afferents, giant interneurons, and dorsal unpaired median (DUM) neurons, whose intrinsic pacemaker activity is strongly modulated by multiple neurotransmitter systems (Pollack et al. 1988; Dubreil et al. 1994; Geffard et al. 1996). nAChR receptors are not only present in synapses between sensory neurons and giant interneurons, but also they are widely expressed in DUM neurons, which influence spontaneous activity of the escape system of the cockroach.

Although MG 624 has not been extensively characterized in insects, its pharmacological activity is known to be associated with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Therefore, the increase in spontaneous activity observed in the present study is more likely to reflect the complexity of cholinergic regulation within the cockroach neural network than a non-specific action of the compound. In particular, the documented involvement of nicotinic receptors in the modulation of DUM neuron excitability (Grolleau et al. 1996) provides a plausible mechanism through which nicotinic receptor blockade may alter the overall spontaneous activity recorded from the abdominal connectives. Therefore, the increase in spontaneous firing observed after MG 624 administration may reflect network-level effects resulting from modulation of cholinergic signaling within the escape circuitry rather than a simple reduction of excitatory transmission. The subsequent return toward control levels suggests the involvement of compensatory mechanisms or additional receptor populations contributing to the regulation of spontaneous activity.

Capsaicin, in contrast, significantly reduced spontaneous neural activity, consistent with recent findings that capsaicin can inhibit slow-inactivating sodium currents in P. americana neurons (Kamezaki and Nishiwaki 2025).

When capsaicin was applied in the presence of MG 624, the reduction in spontaneous firing was no longer observed. We acknowledge that, because MG 624 alone exerted a pronounced effect on spontaneous activity, the present data do not allow us to determine whether nicotinic receptor signaling is required for the electrophysiological action of capsaicin. The absence of a capsaicin-induced decrease in activity following MG 624 treatment may reflect an interaction between cholinergic signaling and the mechanisms engaged by capsaicin. However, an alternative explanation is that the strong effect of MG 624 on network activity obscured the suppressive action of capsaicin. Therefore, our data support an interaction between MG 624-sensitive pathways and capsaicin-induced neuronal modulation, but they do not establish the precise nature of this interaction.

Behavioral data are consistent with, and complement the electrophysiological observations, suggesting that the interactions between TRP-dependent signaling and cholinergic pathways may contribute to thermoregulatory behavior. Consistent with our previous report (Maliszewska et al. 2018), capsaicin induced a shift toward cooler ambient temperatures and reduces head temperature, paralleling hypothermic and heat-avoidance responses observed in mammals following TRPV1 activation (Szolcsányi 2015). In cockroaches, capsaicin promotes selection of cooler environments. Importantly, these thermoregulatory effects were abolished when nicotinic receptors were blocked with MG 624. Moreover, the behavioral response to capsazepine, a TRPV1 antagonist, was likewise attenuated by nicotinic blockade. Together, these findings suggest that cholinergic signaling contributes to the behavioral consequences of TRP receptor modulation. It should be noted that, in the groups receiving combined treatments, capsaicin or capsazepine was applied after the start of the behavioral assay. While vehicle controls indicate that the application procedure alone was not sufficient to induce the observed changes in thermopreference, a minor contribution of handling or application-related effects cannot be entirely excluded and should be considered when interpreting these results.

A further point to consider is that the electrophysiological and behavioral experiments differed in the route of drug administration and level of biological organization. In the electrophysiological experiments, compounds were applied to a semi-isolated preparation in which the ventral nerve cord was exposed while peripheral sensory structures remained intact, allowing access to both central and peripheral neural elements. In contrast, capsaicin, capsazepine, and MG 624 were applied externally in the behavioral assays. Although numerous biologically active compounds are known to penetrate the insect cuticle and affect internal target tissues (Tak and Isman 2015; Yahouédo et al. 2027), the present experiments do not allow us to determine where capsaicin, capsazepine, or MG 624 exerted their primary effect. Consequently, it remains unclear whether the observed behavioral responses resulted from action on peripheral sensory structures, central neural circuits, or a combination of both. The results clearly show that interference with nicotinic signaling alters the thermoregulatory effects of TRP ligands, however the exact anatomical site at which these interactions occur remains to be established.

Grooming behavior provided additional insight into the neurochemical pathways involved. In insects, grooming is strongly influenced by neuromodulators. For example, monoaminergic manipulation can profoundly alter grooming patterns; reserpine-induced monoamine depletion elicits intense grooming in cockroaches (Liebersat and Pflueger 2004), and octopamine enhances leg grooming (Carrazoni et al. 2016). We previously demonstrated that capsaicin elevates octopamine levels and increases leg grooming in P. americana (Maliszewska et al. 2024). In the present study, capsaicin produced only minor changes in antennal grooming but markedly increased leg grooming. MG 624 alone strongly enhanced antennal grooming, whereas combined MG 624 and capsaicin treatment did not further augment this parameter. In contrast, leg grooming progressively increased across treatments, with the highest values observed under combined exposure. These divergent patterns suggest that antennal and leg grooming are governed by partially distinct neural circuits and receptor populations. Although dopamine and octopamine are well established modulators of grooming behavior (Novikova and Zhukovskaya 2015; Borbor et al. 2025), comparatively little is known about the role of acetylcholine. Studies in honeybees have shown that acetylcholinesterase inhibitors increase grooming activity (Williamson et al. 2013), indicating that cholinergic signaling may influence motor stereotypies. Because MG 624 selectively targets α7-containing receptors without affecting other subtypes such as α4β2- or α3β4-like receptors, differential receptor distribution may account for the distinct grooming responses observed between antennae and legs. It is also plausible that capsaicin-induced octopaminergic modulation exerts a stronger influence on leg grooming, thereby overshadowing cholinergic effects in this behavioral domain.

Despite pronounced electrophysiological and behavioral alterations, neither capsaicin, capsazepine, nor MG 624 significantly affected whole-animal metabolic rate. This finding indicates that modulation of neural excitability and thermoregulatory behavior does not necessarily translate into measurable changes in global energy expenditure under the present experimental conditions. The absence of metabolic effects suggests that the observed responses primarily reflect neural circuit reconfiguration rather than systemic metabolic adjustments.

Collectively, our results indicate that cholinergic signaling contributes to behavioral responses induced by TRP ligands in P. americana and that both capsaicin and nicotinic receptor blockade can modulate neuronal activity within the cockroach nervous system. While the electrophysiological and behavioral experiments address different levels of biological organization and do not establish a direct mechanistic link between peripheral thermosensory signaling and central neuronal modulation, they collectively highlight interactions between TRP ligand-dependent responses and cholinergic pathways. The present findings suggest that nicotinic acetylcholine receptors influence the behavioral effects of capsaicin and capsazepine, although the precise site and mechanism of this interaction remain to be determined. Further studies will be required to establish how TRP-dependent sensory signals are integrated with cholinergic neurotransmission in the neural circuits underlying thermoregulatory behavior in insects.

X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (XLHED; Christ–Siemens–Touraine syndrome, ICD-10: Q82.4) is the most common type of ectodermal dysplasia, caused by genetic disorders of ectodermal derivatives. The condition significantly impacts patients’ quality of life, presenting with a classic triad of hypohidrosis, hypotrichosis and hypodontia, which creates a risk of impaired thermoregulation and necessitates complex dental rehabilitation. The molecular basis of the disease lies in alterations of the EDA gene, which encodes ectodysplasin A. This protein belongs to the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) family and plays a critical signaling role in ectodermal-mesenchymal interactions during embryonic development. The present case report describes a boy with an XLHED phenotype caused by a previously unreported structural rearrangement. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) identified a ~397.3 kb microduplication at the Xq13.1 locus directly involving the EDA gene. Comprehensive bioinformatic analysis ruled out additional pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other genes that could account for the patient’s phenotype. The Xq13.1 microduplication was confirmed in both the proband and his mother using quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR). Androgen receptor (AR) gene methylation analysis in the mother revealed a random X-chromosome inactivation (74/26 %), explaining her asymptomatic carrier status. The proband’s clinical manifestations were also compared to those of literature-reported patients with overlapping genomic rearrangements. Based on international and Russian guidelines for the interpretation of massively parallel sequencing data, the identified variant was classified as pathogenic. Identification of this structural rearrangement expands the known mutational spectrum of the EDA gene. Establishing a precise molecular genetic diagnosis in this family is critical not only for disease verification but also for optimizing patient management through a multidisciplinary approach. Furthermore, it enables comprehensive genetic counseling, identification of female carriers among relatives and the development of timely primary and secondary prevention measures for the disease in this family.

X-сцепленная гипогидротическая эктодермальная дисплазия (синдром Криста–Сименса–Турена, МКБ-10: Q82.4) представляет собой наиболее распространенную форму эктодермальной дисплазии, вызванной наследственными нарушениями развития производных эктодермы. Заболевание существенно влияет на качество жизни пациентов, проявляясь классической триадой симптомов: гипогидрозом, гипотрихозом и гиподонтией, что создает риски нарушения терморегуляции и требует сложной стоматологической реабилитации. Молекулярной основой патологии служат нарушения в гене EDA, ответственном за синтез эктодисплазина-А. Данный белок принадлежит к семейству фактора некроза опухоли (TNF) и играет критическую сигнальную роль в процессе эктодермально-мезенхимальных взаимодействий во время эмбрионального развития. В настоящей работе описан клинический случай мальчика с фенотипом X-сцепленной гипогидротической эктодермальной дисплазии, обусловленный ранее не описанной структурной перестройкой. Методом полногеномного секвенирования (WGS) была выявлена микродупликация локуса Xq13.1 размером приблизительно 397.3 Кб, непосредственно затрагивающая ген EDA. Комплексный биоинформатический анализ подтвердил отсутствие дополнительных патогенных или вероятно патогенных вариантов в других генах, которые могли обусловливать фенотип пациента. Микродупликация Xq13.1 подтверждена у пробанда и его матери методом количественной полимеразной цепной реакции в режиме реального времени. Анализ метилирования гена AR продемонстрировал у матери равновероятную инактивацию X-хромосомы (74/26 %), что объясняет ее бессимптомное носительство. Проведено сравнение клинических проявлений пробанда с описанными в литературе пациентами, имеющими близкие по координатам структурные перестройки. На основании международных и российских руководств по интерпретации данных массового параллельного секвенирования обнаруженный вариант классифицирован как патогенный. Идентификация этой структурной перестройки расширяет известный мутационный спектр гена EDA. Уточнение молекулярно-генетического диагноза в описанной семье имеет критическое значение не только для верификации нозологии, но и для коррекции тактики ведения пациента, включая междисциплинарный подход к лечению. Кроме того, это позволяет провести качественное медико-генетическое консультирование, выявить носительство у родственников женского пола и разработать эффективные меры первичной и вторичной профилактики заболевания в данной семье.

Introduction

Ectodermal dysplasia is a genetically and clinically heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by defects in two or more ectodermal derivatives, including sweat glands, hair, and teeth (Visinoni et al., 2009). Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is a subgroup of ectodermal dysplasias, whose characteristic clinical feature is reduced sweat gland function, leading to impaired thermoregulation (Anbouba et al., 2020; Wohlfart et al., 2020). Pathogenic variants in four genes account for approximately 90 % of hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia cases: EDA (X-linked forms), EDAR and EDARADD (responsible for both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive forms), and WNT10A (autosomal recessive forms) (Cluzeau et al., 2011).

X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (Christ–Siemens– Touraine syndrome, XLHED) (OMIM: #305100) is a hereditary disorder affecting structures of ectodermal origin, such as hair, teeth, nails, and sweat glands. The disease is caused by pathogenic variants in the EDA gene, responsible for the synthesis of the protein ectodysplasin A. This protein belongs to the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) family of ligands and plays an important role in the formation of ectodermderived structures during embryogenesis (Kere et al., 1996; Mikkola, Thesleff, 2003). According to the literature, X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is the most common form of hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia worldwide (Lamartine, 2003). The prevalence of this disease is estimated to range from 1 to 22 per 100,000 individuals (Cañueto et al., 2011; Nguyen-Nielsen et al., 2013). The clinical presentation of this disease involves various combinations of the following features: hypohidrosis, hypotrichosis, and hypodontia (Itin, Fistarol, 2004; Bagdey et al., 2022). This paper presents a clinical case involving an Xq13.1 duplication not described hitherto.

Materials and methods

A family with a suspected case of ectodermal dysplasia in the son was enrolled in this study. The research was conducted in compliance with ethical standards as outlined in the World Medical Association’s Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from all participating family members. The study protocol was approved by the Biomedical Ethics Committee of the Research Institute of Medical Genetics, Tomsk National Research Medical Center (Protocol No. 10, dated January 20, 2021).

Peripheral blood samples were collected from the patient and his parents into EDTA-containing tubes for molecular genetic analysis. Genomic DNA was extracted from whole blood using the standard phenol-chloroform method.

Whole-genome sequencing of the proband was performed within the collaborative research program with the National Genetic Initiative “100,000+Me” at Biotech Campus Company. Whole-genome sequencing was carried out on DNBSEQ-T7 platforms (MGI) using the MGIEasy FS PCR-Free Library Prep Set (MGI) for library preparation, producing 2 × 150 bp paired-end reads. The bioinformatics pipeline included adapter trimming and quality filtering of raw data, followed by alignment of reads to the GRCh38 reference genome using BWA-MEM v0.7.17 (http://bio-bwa.sourceforge.net/). Duplicate reads were marked using GATK MarkDuplicates v4.3.0.0 (McKenna et al., 2010). Single nucleotide variants and small indels were called using DeepVariant v4.0.0. For each sample, the fraction of reads with a quality score of at least Q30 was ≥90 % of the total reads obtained by sequencing.

Variant annotation was performed using Annovar (Wang et al., 2010). The clinical relevance of identified variants was assessed using the OMIM (http://www.omim.org/), ClinVar (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/), gnomAD v4.1.0 exomes (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/), HPO (https:// hpo.jax.org/), and Decipher (https://www.deciphergenomics. org/) databases, as well as data from the scientific literature

To validate the Xq13.1 microduplication, quantitative real-time PCR was performed on DNA from the proband and his parents using the following primer pairs (Syntol, Russia): targeting exon 2 of the EDA gene (F: 5ʹ-TGGCT ATGACTGAGTGGGGT-3ʹ; R: 5ʹ-GCTTCTTTTATTGC GGCGAAC-3ʹ) and targeting intron 1 of the EDA gene (F: 5ʹ-GTGGGATGTTGGAGGAACT-3ʹ; R: 5ʹ-TGCGAAC TTTGGTGAAGAAGC-3ʹ).

Primers were designed using the Primer-BLAST resource (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/tools/primer-blast/). Selected primer sequences were tested for the formation of hairpins, self- and heterodimers using the OligoAnalyzer tool (https:// eu.idtdna.com/calc/analyzer).

The X-chromosome inactivation status was determined by amplifying a highly polymorphic CAG repeat in the first exon of the androgen receptor gene (AR, Xq12) after DNA hydrolysis with the methylation-sensitive restriction endonuclease HpaII. PCR products were separated using fragment analysis. An inactivation skewing of less than 80 % was considered a random pattern of X-chromosome inactivation, whereas a skewing of more than 80 % was regarded as indicative of skewed (asymmetric) X-chromosome inactivation (sXCI) (Allen et al., 1992).

Results

Clinical case report. The proband, a 14-year-old male, was examined at the Genetic Clinic of the Research Institute of Medical Genetics, Tomsk National Research Medical Center, due to suspected anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia. His medical history was significant for congenital absence of sweating and impaired thermoregulation. At the age of two months, he was diagnosed with atopic dermatitis and subsequently followed up for this condition, which was characterized by recurrent episodes of acute allergic manifestations, including atopic dermatitis and urticaria, requiring numerous hospitalizations in early childhood. His primary dentition erupted at 8 months of age and was notable for conical (awl-shaped) teeth.

The initial diagnosis of Christ–Siemens–Touraine syndrome with an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern was established at the age of 1 year and 5 months following a consultation by a clinical geneticist, based on the characteristic clinical presentation.

At the age of 2 years, the patient developed phimosis with the formation of synechiae. At 6 years, the proband was admitted to a surgical hospital with a diagnosis of acute balanoposthitis and preputial synechiae. From the age of 7 years, he has been followed up by a neurologist for an obsessivecompulsive disorder and a localized motor tic involving the periorbital musculature.

During a follow-up examination by a clinical geneticist at the age of 14, the following phenotypic features were noted: hypodontia of the upper jaw with conical teeth, anodontia of the lower jaw, hypotrichosis, periorbital hyperpigmentation, and palmoplantar keratoderma. The patient was subsequently referred for molecular genetic confirmation of the diagnosis.

Whole-genome sequencing identified a hemizygous ~397.3 kb duplication on chromosome X, spanning approximate coordinates chrX:69,620,777–70,018,072 and affecting the disease‑associated EDA gene (Fig. 1).

Fig. 1. Proband NGS sequencing (IGV browser).

The Xq13.1 microduplication was confirmed in the proband and his mother by quantitative real-time PCR (Fig. 2). Neither of the proband’s parents exhibited any clinical manifestations of the disease.

Fig. 2. Copy number analysis of the Xq13.1 region in the proband and his parents. Results of real-time PCR assays targeting intron 1 and exon 2 of the EDA gene.

The X-axis represents the male control sample, proband, mother, and father; the Y-axis shows the relative DNA copy number change.

The proband’s parents showed no clinical manifestations of the disease. Analysis of the X-chromosome inactivation status in the proband’s mother demonstrated random X-chromosome inactivation (74/26 %).

Discussion

The EDA gene spans 419 kb, comprises eight exons, and encodes ectodysplasin A, a signaling ligand of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) family, which plays a key role in the formation of ectodermal structures during embryogenesis. The function of ectodysplasin A is to transmit a positive signal supporting cell survival, proliferation, and differentiation during epithelialmesenchymal interactions, particularly in the development of hair follicles (Laurikkala et al., 2002).

According to the literature, hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is frequently associated with atopic conditions, including atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, and bronchial asthma (Stein, 2007). This association may be explained by impaired barrier function of the skin and mucous membranes, leading to xerosis (dry skin), as well as by thermoregulatory dysfunction resulting from sweat gland abnormalities. Dysfunction of bronchial glands has also been reported, which may predispose individuals to recurrent respiratory infections and bronchitis. In our clinical case, the patient showed signs of atopic dermatitis from the first months of life, requiring medical management.

The clinical presentation in the proband is consistent with the classical phenotype of X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (Itin, Fistarol, 2004). In addition, the clinical features are similar to previously reported cases associated with pathogenic copy number variations (CNVs) affecting the EDA gene, including both deletions (Patient-1, Patient-2) and a duplication (Patient-3) (see the Table).

Note. Sources: a (Hayashi et al., 2013); b (Li et al., 2008); c (Al Marzouqi et al., 2014); N/A – Not Assessed.

According to the literature and genomic databases, three cases of intragenic copy number variations (CNVs) have been described to date: two microdeletions and one microduplication. All of these cases were reported in patients presenting with a pronounced clinical picture consistent with the specific disease phenotype.

In Patient-1 (Hayashi et al., 2013), a deletion was identified and designated as NC_000023.11(NM_001399.5):c.397- 1589_502+13848del. This rearrangement corresponds to an intragenic deletion within the Xq13.1 region, spanning genomic coordinates chrX:69955438-69970980 and involving exon 2 of the EDA gene. In Patient-2 (Li et al., 2008), a 22-bp intragenic deletion was identified within exon 8 of the EDA gene, resulting in a frameshift. In Patient-3 (Al Marzouqi et al., 2014), an intragenic duplication of EDA exon 2 was reported. In addition, a duplication with similar coordinates is registered in the Decipher database (Patient:289747) and classified as pathogenic (Fig. 3).

Fig. 3. Schematic scale-fitted representation of rearrangements in previously reported patients with duplications (blue bars), deletions (red bars), and the proband within the EDA gene.

Structural variants with similar coordinates are not observed in the population frequency databases gnomAD CNVs/ SVs v4.1.0.

According to the ACMG criteria established for the assessment of CNV pathogenicity, this rearrangement is classified as pathogenic, receiving a score of 1.0 (criteria 1A, 2A, 3A) (Riggs et al., 2020). Based on the refined ACMG/AMP criteria adapted for the evaluation of monogenic CNVs, this rearrangement is also classified as pathogenic (PVS1, PM2, PP4) (Brandt et al., 2020).

X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is known to exhibit incomplete penetrance in female carriers due to its X-linked recessive inheritance pattern (Munoz et al., 1997; Cambiaghi et al., 2000). The identified variant was inherited from the mother, who is a heterozygous asymptomatic carrier. Clinical manifestations of X-linked recessive disorders in women may be absent due to the heterozygous state of the X chromosome and random X-chromosome inactivation (Vincent et al., 2001). However, if skewed X-chromosome inactivation is present, female carriers may exhibit clinical symptoms when the homologue carrying the pathogenic variant remains active. In this case, we found random X-chromosome inactivation in the proband’s mother, which explains the absence of clinical manifestations of the disease. This rearrangement is assessed as pathogenic based on a combination of clinical data, pathogenicity criteria, and literature reports

An important aspect of the presented clinical case is the utilization of whole-genome sequencing for the diagnosis of this disease. Verifying an intragenic microduplication on the X chromosome in a male patient using standard NGS approaches (such as targeted gene sequencing or whole-exome sequencing) is extremely challenging. In a male, the hemizygous state of the X chromosome, combined with a copy number gain in a specific region, could be misinterpreted as increased gene coverage, potentially leading to a false negative diagnosis. Furthermore, methods designed to determine DNA copy number, such as MLPA, array CGH, or real-time PCR, are not routinely used in the diagnosis of Christ–Siemens– Touraine syndrome, because pathogenic variants are represented by various single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in up to 90 % of cases.

Conclusion

This report presents a clinical case of X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia caused by a previously unreported ~397.3 kb duplication at Xq13.1, affecting the EDA gene. The duplication breakpoints map to approximately chrX:69,620,777–70,018,072. The diagnosis was established based on the characteristic clinical presentation. Molecular genetic confirmation allowed us to clarify the etiology and identify carrier status in the asymptomatic mother with random X-chromosome inactivation. This finding enables preconception and prenatal diagnostic options for future pregnancies in this family, given the potential for transmission by female carriers.

ABSTRACT

The skin undertakes multiple critical physiological functions, including barrier protection and thermoregulation. However, chronic nonhealing ulcers have emerged as a major clinical challenge. In wound repair, skin healing is a highly coordinated, time‐sequential process wherein fibroblasts—key dermal cells—play irreplaceable roles in proliferation, migration, differentiation, and extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis. When external environmental factors induce fibroblast dysfunction, this can lead to impaired epithelialization, thereby resulting in persistent wound nonclosure, which may represent a key mechanism underlying the pathogenesis of this condition. Yet current clinical treatments (debridement, anti‐infection, negative pressure drainage, and growth factors) fail to resolve this, with high recurrence and poorly understood molecular mechanisms. To this end, we identified in this study a low‑molecular‑weight bioactive peptide (< 10 kDa) originating from Wuguchong (JY), which is capable of specifically regulating fibroblasts in the wound microenvironment. By modulating the Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway, this peptide restores fibroblast function, thereby promoting wound healing and effectively ameliorating the challenge of impaired wound repair. This study not only offers promise for the development of new drugs for treating ulcers, but also provides novel insights and strategies for cell‑based therapies targeting other types of wound healing.

1 Introduction

Skin wound healing is a coordinated biological process involving hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and tissue remodeling [1, 2]. Successful repair requires the timely interaction of multiple cell types and signaling pathways to restore tissue continuity and function [3]. Fibroblasts are particularly important during the proliferative and remodeling phases because they migrate into the injured area, proliferate, produce extracellular matrix (ECM), and contribute to granulation tissue formation [4, 5]. In response to local signals, a subset of fibroblasts differentiates into contractile myofibroblasts, which express α‐smooth muscle actin (α‐SMA), generate mechanical tension, and promote wound contraction [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. Therefore, appropriate regulation of fibroblast proliferation, migration, activation, and matrix synthesis is essential for efficient skin repair.

Although acute cutaneous wounds generally heal through an orderly and self‐limited process, delayed or impaired repair may occur when cellular responses are insufficient, dysregulated, or exposed to unfavorable local conditions [12, 13]. Current wound‐management strategies, including debridement, infection control, negative‐pressure therapy, biological dressings, and growth‐factor‐based interventions, can improve clinical outcomes, but their effectiveness varies according to wound type and patient condition. Identifying natural products that can enhance the activity of key repair cells may therefore provide useful leads for developing new wound‐healing interventions [14, 15, 16, 17].

The Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway is an important regulator of tissue development, homeostasis, and repair [18, 19]. Mammals express three Hh ligands: Sonic hedgehog (Shh), Indian hedgehog (Ihh), and Desert hedgehog (Dhh), which have distinct biological functions. In the skin, Shh signaling participates in hair follicle cycling, sebaceous gland development, and tissue regeneration [20, 21]. Ihh is mainly associated with chondrocyte proliferation and endochondral ossification, whereas Dhh contributes to testicular development and peripheral nerve organization [22, 23]. In the canonical Hh pathway, ligand binding relieves Patched1 (PTCH1)‐mediated inhibition of Smoothened (SMO), leading to the activation of GLI transcription factors and the expression of downstream genes involved in cell proliferation, survival, and tissue remodeling [24, 25]. Increasing evidence indicates that Hh signaling is activated after skin injury and contributes to dermal fibroblast proliferation, migration, and skin appendage regeneration [21]. These findings suggest that modulation of Hh signaling may influence fibroblast behavior during cutaneous wound repair.

Bioactive substances (such as bioactive peptides [26, 27, 28]) derived from natural sources have attracted considerable interest as potential wound‐healing agents because of their structural diversity and biological activity [29, 30, 31]. Wuguchong (JY), derived from the desiccated larvae of Chrysomya megacephala and related species in the family Calliphoridae, has traditionally been used in wound management. Previous studies have mainly focused on the debridement‐related effects of live maggots or the antimicrobial and other biological activities of crude maggot‐derived preparations [32, 33]. However, there remains a paucity of evidence regarding the components of JY with potential tissue‑repairing activity, as well as their underlying mechanisms.

In the present study, we prepared a JY fraction with a molecular weight below 10 kDa, referred to as JY < 10 kDa, and evaluated its effects on cutaneous wound repair. Using a mouse acute full‐thickness excisional wound model and L929 fibroblast‐based assays, we examined wound closure, tissue regeneration, fibroblast proliferation and migration, fibroblast activation, and collagen production. We further investigated the involvement of the Hh pathway by analyzing PTCH1, GLI1, and Cyclin D1 expression and by using the SMO inhibitor vismodegib. This study aims to clarify the potential role of JY < 10 kDa in acute skin wound healing and to determine whether Hh pathway‐associated regulation of fibroblast function contributes to its biological activity.

2 Materials and Methods

2.1 Experimental Animals

Twenty SPF‐grade male C57BL/6 mice (22–24 g) were obtained from Cyagen Biosciences (Gu'an, China) and housed under standard conditions at the Experimental Animal Center of Dalian Medical University, with ad libitum access to food and water. All procedures complied with the Regulations for the Administration of Laboratory Animals issued by the State Science and Technology Commission of China.

2.2 Experimental Cells and Treatment

The mouse fibroblast L929 cell line (CVCL_0462, iCell‐m026) was obtained from Shanghai Saibai Kang Biotechnology Co. Ltd. (China) and cultured in Eagle's Minimum Essential Medium (MEM) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. L929 were treated with JY solution and Hh pathway inhibitor vismodegib (10 µM) for 24 h [34].

2.3 Preparation of JY < 10 KDa Bioactive Component

Wuguchong (JY) is derived from the desiccated larvae of C. megacephala and other allied species within the family Calliphoridae. The dried JY insect used in this study was sourced from Leshan, Sichuan Province, China. The production license (Liao 20150128) was issued by Dalian Medical University School of Pharmacy, and it was identified and provided by them (product number: 241101). Dried JY (100 g) was weighed, ground, and extracted by refluxing with 300 mL triple‐distilled water at 70 °C three times (1 h each). The combined supernatants were concentrated by rotary evaporation and lyophilized. The crude extract was redissolved in water (< 100 mg/mL), filtered through membranes (0.22 µm), and ultrafiltered using a 10 kDa centrifugal filter (4500 × g, 40 min). The filtrate (JY<10 kDa) and retentate (JY > 10 kDa) were collected separately and lyophilized for subsequent use. The 10 kDa as a bioactive fraction containing small molecules (primarily peptides).

For in vitro assays, the total aqueous extract of JY and its JY > 10 kDa and JY < 10 kDa fractions were dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as 256 mg/mL stock solutions, the final concentration of DMSO was 0.1% (v/v), and their protein contents were determined using the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay. For in vivo experiments, JY powder was dissolved in a glycerol–water vehicle (1:1, v/v) to concentrations of 15, 30, and 60 mg/mL. Each wound was treated with 0.1 mL of formulation containing JY solution at concentrations corresponding to final doses of 15, 30, and 60 mg/kg. Kangfuxin Liquid (Tianshuxin), a commercial preparation of ethanol extract from the dried body of Periplaneta americana L., was purchased from Hunan Kelun Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (Yueyang, Hunan, China; approval No. Z43020995; Lot No. M240317) and used as the positive control as received, and each wound was treated with 0.1 mL. All formulations were prepared fresh before use, vortexed, and applied topically to wound sites.

2.4 Animal Grouping, Model Establishment, and Treatment

All animal procedures were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Dalian Medical University (Approval No. XL250610065). Mice were anesthetized, and after loss of the pain reflex was confirmed, the dorsal hair was shaved. A full‐thickness excisional wound (1 cm in diameter) was created on the dorsal skin using sterile surgical scissors. The mice were randomly divided into five groups (n = 4): vehicle control (glycerol–water, 1:1, v/v), low‑dose (15 mg/kg), medium‑dose (30 mg/kg), high‑dose (60 mg/kg) JY < 10 kDa, and a positive control (Kangfuxin Liquid). Each wound received a daily topical application of 200 µL of the corresponding formulation for 7 consecutive days. Wound healing was monitored by photography on days 0, 3, 5, and 7. Wound areas were measured using ImageJ, and the healing rate was calculated as follows: Healingrate%=Initial area−Area on dayn/Initial area×100%.

Statistical analysis was performed using one‑way ANOVA. On day 7, all mice were euthanized, and skin tissue from the wound area was collected for subsequent histological and molecular analysis.

2.5 Histological and Immunological Analyses

2.5.1 Hematoxylin–Eosin (H&E) Staining and Masson Staining

Skin tissue samples harvested on day 7 were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h, dehydrated through a graded ethanol series, cleared in xylene, and embedded in paraffin [35]. Sections (5–8 µm) were prepared for staining. For hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated, stained with hematoxylin (5 min), differentiated in 1% acid ethanol (30 s), blued in running water (10 min), and counterstained with eosin (1.5–3 min). After dehydration and clearing, sections were mounted. For Masson's trichrome staining, sections were baked at 65°C for 2 h, deparaffinized, and rehydrated. Staining was performed sequentially with 2.5% potassium dichromate, hematoxylin, ponceau acid fuchsin, 1% phosphomolybdic acid (differentiation), and aniline blue. Sections were then dehydrated, cleared, and mounted. All stained sections were examined under a light microscope to evaluate inflammatory cell infiltration, epithelial regeneration, and collagen deposition.

2.5.2 Immunohistochemistry and Immunofluorescence Staining

For immunohistochemistry (IHC), deparaffinized and rehydrated tissue sections underwent antigen retrieval and were blocked with 5% BSA for 30 min, followed by incubation with primary antibodies (α‐SMA and Collagen I) at 4°C overnight and then with HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. For immunofluorescence (IF) staining of L929 cells, after fixation with 4% paraformaldehyde and permeabilization with 0.1% Triton X‐100, cells were blocked and incubated with anti‐PCNA primary antibody at 4°C overnight, followed by appropriate fluorescent secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. In both procedures, nuclei were counterstained with DAPI, mounted with anti‐fade medium, and visualized under a fluorescence microscope.

2.6 Cell Function Assays

2.6.1 EdU Proliferation Assay

L929 cells were seeded in 96‐well plates at 1 × 105 cells/mL, adhered for 24 h, and then serum‐starved in fresh serum‐free medium for an additional 24 h. After starvation, cells were treated with various concentrations of JY < 10 kDa for 24 h. Cell proliferation was assessed using an EdU assay kit, where cells were incubated with EdU, fixed, and stained with a fluorescent azide conjugate. Nuclei were counterstained with Hoechst 33342. Images were acquired by fluorescence microscopy, and the percentage of EdU‐positive cells was quantified to determine the proliferation rate.

2.6.2 Scratch Wound Healing Assay and Transwell Migration Assay

For the scratch wound healing assay, L929 cells were seeded in six‐well plates and cultured to approximately 80% confluence. A uniform scratch was made with a sterile 200 µL pipette tip. After washing with PBS, cells were treated with various concentrations of JY < 10 kDa. Scratch images were taken at 0 and 24 h, and the migration rate was quantified by measuring the reduction in scratch area. For the transwell migration assay, L929 cells in serum‐free medium were seeded into the upper chamber of a 24‐well transwell plate (8 µm pores), with the lower chamber containing medium with 20% FBS as a chemoattractant. After 24 h, nonmigrated cells were removed, and cells on the lower surface were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, stained with 0.1% crystal violet, visualized under an inverted microscope, and counted in five random fields per well.

2.7 Western Blot Analysis

Tissue homogenates or cultured cells were lysed with RIPA buffer containing protease inhibitors, and total protein was extracted by centrifugation. Protein concentration was determined using a BCA assay. Equal amounts of protein (20–30 µg per lane) were separated by SDS‐PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes. After blocking with 5% non‐fat milk in TBST for 2 h at room temperature, membranes were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against PTCH1, GLI1, Cyclin D1, α‐SMA, Collagen I, PCNA, and β‐Actin (loading control). Following washes with TBST, membranes were incubated with HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies for 1.5 h at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using an ECL reagent, and band intensities were quantified by densitometric analysis with ImageJ software.

2.8 Statistical Analysis

All quantitative data are expressed as mean ± SD from at least three independent experiments. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0. Differences among multiple groups were analyzed by one‐way ANOVA followed by a suitable post‐hoc test, while comparisons between two groups were conducted using an unpaired, two‐tailed Student's t‐test. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

3 Results and Discussion

3.1 JY < 10 kDa Component Promotes Fibroblast Viability and is Identified as the Core Active Fraction

To identify the bioactive fraction of JY, the aqueous extract was separated by ultrafiltration into fractions with molecular weights below and above 10 kDa. The JY<10 kDa fraction was subsequently characterized by MALDI‐TOF mass spectrometry. The detected molecular‐weight distribution ranged from 113.65 to 9108 Da, with prominent signals at 3196.04, 6583, and 7195 Da (Figures 1A and S1). These data confirm that JY < 10 kDa is a heterogeneous low‐molecular‐weight fraction rather than a single purified compound. Accordingly, the term “JY < 10 kDa fraction” is used throughout this manuscript rather than implying that the material represents one defined small molecule or a single peptide.

The effects of the JY fractions on L929 fibroblasts were evaluated using the CCK‐8 assay. JY<10 kDa increased fibroblast viability in a concentration‐dependent manner, with the most pronounced effect observed at 64 µg/mL and no apparent cytotoxicity under the tested conditions (Figure 1B,C). These findings identify JY<10 kDa as the principal fibroblast‐active fraction of the crude extract. The relatively low molecular‐weight distribution may be advantageous for tissue penetration and formulation development; however, the specific constituents responsible for the observed activity remain to be determined. Further chromatographic separation, high‐resolution mass spectrometry, peptide sequencing where appropriate, and nuclear magnetic resonance analysis will be required to define the active chemical entities and their structure–activity relationships.

The identification of a fibroblast‐active fraction provides a mechanistic extension of the traditional use of JY in wound management. Historically, the beneficial effects of medicinal maggots have been associated mainly with biological debridement, in which live larvae remove necrotic tissue and secrete proteolytic enzymes [36]. Increasing evidence indicates that maggot‐derived preparations may also exert antimicrobial, anti‐inflammatory, angiogenic, and tissue‐reparative effects [32, 33]. The present results suggest that the low‐molecular‐weight fraction contributes directly to wound repair by acting on fibroblasts, which are essential effector cells during granulation tissue formation and ECM remodeling.

3.2 JY < 10 kDa Accelerates Wound Closure and Improves Tissue Regeneration In Vivo

The wound‐healing activity of JY < 10 kDa was then examined in a mouse full‐thickness excisional wound model. Topical treatment accelerated wound closure in a dose‐dependent manner compared with the vehicle control (Figure 2A,B). By day 7, the high‐dose JY < 10 kDa group exhibited a healing rate comparable to that of the positive‐control group treated with Kangfuxin liquid, and both groups showed a statistically significant reduction in wound area relative to the model control (p < 0.05). These findings demonstrate that the JY < 10 kDa fraction retains substantial reparative activity in vivo and that its effect is not restricted to cultured fibroblasts.

Histological examination provided further evidence of improved tissue repair. Compared with the vehicle‐treated wounds, JY < 10 kDa‐treated wounds displayed more advanced re‐epithelialization, greater epithelial thickness, and more prominent granulation tissue formation, together with reduced inflammatory‐cell infiltration (Figures 2C and S2). Masson's trichrome staining additionally showed increased deposition and improved organization of collagen fibers in the treatment groups (Figures 2D and S3). These histological changes are consistent with accelerated progression through the proliferative phase of healing, during which fibroblast recruitment, granulation tissue formation, and ECM deposition are central events.

The reduction in inflammatory‐cell infiltration is also notable. Although the present study did not directly characterize inflammatory‐cell subsets or inflammatory mediators, excessive or persistent inflammation is a recognized barrier to effective wound closure [37]. The histological findings therefore raise the possibility that JY < 10 kDa may indirectly modulate the wound microenvironment while directly enhancing fibroblast function. This possibility should be investigated in future studies by examining macrophage polarization, inflammatory cytokines, neutrophil persistence, and the resolution phase of inflammation. As the current model simulates acute wounds in healthy mice, the observed outcomes should not be construed as evidence of therapeutic efficacy against chronic ulcers, given that chronic ulcers are characterized by hyperglycemia, hypoxia, vascular impairment, sustained inflammation, and bacterial biofilm, all of which may differentially affect the healing process.

3.3 JY < 10 kDa Promotes Wound Healing by Enhancing Fibroblast Activation and Collagen Production

Fibroblasts are recruited to injured tissue, where they proliferate, migrate, produce ECM, and differentiate into myofibroblasts [6]. These processes support granulation tissue formation, wound contraction, and restoration of dermal structure [7, 8, 9, 10]. To elucidate the mechanism through which the JY < 10 kDa fraction modulates fibroblast activity to facilitate wound healing, the expression levels of α‑smooth muscle actin (α‑SMA), type I collagen, and proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) were assessed in the wound tissues [10, 11].

Immunohistochemical analysis showed weak α‐SMA and type I collagen staining in the vehicle‐control group. In contrast, JY < 10 kDa treatment increased both the density and staining intensity of α‐SMA‐positive cells and enhanced the expression and distribution of type I collagen within the granulation tissue in a dose‐dependent manner (Figures 3A,B, S4, and S5). Western blotting produced consistent results, demonstrating increased levels of PCNA, α‐SMA, and type I collagen in JY<10 kDa‐treated wounds (Figure 3C,D). The relative α‐SMA expression in the high‐dose group reached 3.68 ± 0.25 and was significantly higher than that in the control group (**p < 0.001).

These findings indicate that JY < 10 kDa promotes the expansion and activation of fibroblastic cells in the wound bed and enhances matrix deposition. PCNA upregulation is consistent with increased proliferative activity, whereas α‐SMA induction suggests an increase in the myofibroblast‐like phenotype. Type I collagen is a major structural component of the repaired dermis and is required for the development of tensile strength. Nevertheless, α‐SMA expression should be interpreted as evidence of myofibroblast activation rather than as a direct measurement of complete fibroblast differentiation or contractile function. Likewise, increased collagen accumulation may be beneficial during the proliferative phase but could contribute to excessive scarring if it persists during remodeling. Longitudinal analysis of collagen turnover, scar architecture, and wound tensile strength will therefore be important for assessing the quality of repair.

3.4 JY < 10 kDa Stimulates Fibroblast Proliferation, Migration, and Activation In Vitro

To determine whether the tissue‐level effects were attributable to a direct action on fibroblasts, the effects of JY < 10 kDa were evaluated in L929 cells. EdU incorporation and PCNA immunofluorescence demonstrated that JY < 10 kDa significantly increased fibroblast proliferative activity (Figure 4A). This result is consistent with the increased PCNA expression observed in treated wound tissue and supports the interpretation that JY < 10 kDa enhances the fibroblast population available for tissue repair.

The effect of JY < 10 kDa on fibroblast migration was assessed using complementary scratch and transwell assays. In the scratch assay, JY < 10 kDa accelerated the reduction of the cell‐free area over 24 h, indicating enhanced lateral migration and/or repopulation of the injured region (Figure 4B). The transwell assay similarly showed an increased number of cells migrating through the porous membrane toward the serum‐containing lower chamber (Figure 4C). The agreement between these two assays strengthens the conclusion that JY < 10 kDa promotes fibroblast motility.

Western blotting further revealed concentration‐dependent increases in PCNA, α‐SMA, type I collagen, and type III collagen in JY < 10 kDa‐treated L929 cells (Figure 4D). Type III collagen is especially relevant during early granulation tissue formation, whereas type I collagen becomes increasingly important during matrix maturation and restoration of tissue strength. Thus, the coordinated induction of α‐SMA and collagen proteins suggests that JY < 10 kDa enhances several complementary fibroblast functions rather than merely increasing cell number. Together, the in vitro findings provide a cellular explanation for the enhanced granulation tissue formation and collagen deposition observed in vivo.

Fibroblasts are heterogeneous and can display distinct phenotypes according to their anatomical origin, developmental lineage, and local wound signals. The L929 cell line provides a useful model for evaluating general fibroblast responses but does not reproduce the full cellular heterogeneity of human skin. Future studies using primary dermal fibroblasts, papillary and reticular fibroblast subpopulations, and human wound‐derived cells will be needed to determine whether JY < 10 kDa preferentially targets a specific fibroblast state.

3.5 JY < 10 kDa Activates the Hh Signaling Pathway

The Hh pathway is involved in tissue development, homeostasis, fibroblast behavior, and skin repair [24, 25]. To investigate whether Hh signaling contributes to the activity of JY < 10 kDa, the levels of PTCH1, GLI1, and Cyclin D1 were examined in wound tissue and L929 fibroblasts.

In wound tissue, JY < 10 kDa increased PTCH1, GLI1, and Cyclin D1 protein expression in a concentration‐dependent manner (Figure 5A,B). Similar changes were observed in L929 cells treated with JY < 10 kDa (Figure 5C,D). GLI1 is a widely used transcriptional readout of Hh pathway activity, while Cyclin D1 is a downstream cell‐cycle regulator that may connect Hh activation with fibroblast proliferation. PTCH1 is a negative‐feedback receptor whose transcription is also induced by Hh signaling. Therefore, the simultaneous elevation of GLI1, PTCH1, and Cyclin D1 is consistent with activation of Hh pathway‐associated transcriptional responses and provides a plausible molecular link between JY < 10 kDa treatment and the observed increases in fibroblast proliferation and activation.

The present experiments did not directly measure Hh ligand levels, SMO localization, GLI1 transcriptional activity, or primary‐cilium events. This will be further explored in our future research.

3.6 JY < 10 kDa Promotes Fibroblast Activation via the Hh Pathway

To determine whether Hh signaling is functionally required for the effects of JY < 10 kDa, L929 cells were treated with JY < 10 kDa at 64 µg/mL alone or in combination with the SMO inhibitor vismodegib at 10 µM. JY < 10 kDa significantly increased EdU incorporation, whereas co‐treatment with vismodegib markedly reduced this proliferative response (Figure 6A). Similarly, the enhanced scratch closure and transwell migration induced by JY < 10 kDa were substantially attenuated by Hh pathway inhibition (Figure 6B,C). The molecular findings were consistent with the functional assays. JY<10 kDa increased PCNA, α‐SMA, and type I collagen expression, whereas vismodegib co‐treatment suppressed these changes (Figure 6D,E). These rescue experiments indicate that Hh signaling is not merely correlated with JY < 10 kDa treatment but contributes functionally to the regulation of fibroblast proliferation, migration, activation, and matrix production. Taken together, the data support the following working model: the JY < 10 kDa fraction activates Hh pathway‐associated signaling in fibroblasts, leading to increased GLI1‐related transcriptional activity and induction of cell‐cycle and repair‐associated proteins such as Cyclin D1, PCNA, α‐SMA, and collagen. The resulting enhancement of fibroblast proliferation, migration, myofibroblast‐like activation, and ECM production contributes to accelerated wound closure and improved tissue regeneration (Figure 7).

4 Conclusions

In a mouse full‐thickness skin wound model, JY < 10 kDa significantly accelerated wound closure, reduced inflammatory cell infiltration, promoted granulation tissue formation, and enhanced collagen deposition, demonstrating considerable therapeutic potential. In vivo and in vitro analyses verified that JY < 10 kDa upregulates the expression of α‐SMA, PCNA, and collagen, thereby enhancing fibroblast proliferation and activation and accelerating acute wound healing.

Further investigation demonstrated that JY < 10 kDa activates the Hh signaling pathway, which regulates fibroblast proliferation, activation, and collagen production. Rescue experiments using a Hh pathway inhibitor [34] confirmed that this pathway is essential for the observed effects, establishing it as a key mechanism underlying JY < 10 kDa‐induced wound healing.

In summary, this study elucidates that JY < 10 kDa promotes full‐thickness skin wound healing by activating the Hh signaling pathway, which in turn enhances fibroblast proliferation, activation, and collagen synthesis. Our findings systematically clarify the Hh‐fibroblast axis as a central mechanistic pathway and provide a novel strategic foundation for developing natural product‐based therapeutics for wound management.

5 Limitations

This study has several limitations. First, JY < 10 kDa is a heterogeneous low‐molecular‐weight fraction, and its precise chemical composition, peptide sequences, and active constituents remain unidentified. Further bioactivity‐guided fractionation and LC‐MS/MS analysis are required. Second, the experiments used a small number of healthy male mice with acute wounds and a short observation period; therefore, the findings cannot yet be extrapolated to chronic diabetic, ischemic, infected, or otherwise refractory wounds. Third, the study primarily examined L929 fibroblasts and did not determine whether JY < 10 kDa selectively affects fibroblasts or also regulates keratinocytes [38], endothelial cells [39, 40], macrophages [41, 42], or other wound‐related cells. Fourth, the increased expression of PTCH1, GLI1, and Cyclin D1, together with the inhibitory effect of vismodegib, supports Hh pathway involvement but does not establish direct or exclusive pathway activation. Additional genetic and direct pathway assays are needed. Finally, the dosing parameters, formulation reproducibility, long‐term safety, pharmacokinetics, and effects on scar remodeling and tissue function require further evaluation. Thus, JY < 10 kDa should currently be considered a promising preliminary lead rather than a fully characterized therapeutic candidate.
