The novel psychoactive substance (NPS) phenomenon represents a major global problem. Despite the methodical inclusion of new analogues in lists of controlled drugs, new compounds continue to circulate, frequently resulting in fatal intoxications. The emergence of N-isopropyl butylone (NiPB) in 2024, found as an adulterant in methamphetamine-based products, underscores the rapidly evolving landscape of NPSs. Despite its structural similarity to potent monoamine transporter inhibitors, specific pharmacological data and information on its effects in consumers are currently lacking. This study aims to characterize the acute physiological, behavioural, and sensorimotor effects of NiPB (0.1–60 mg/kg; i.p.) in male mice, complemented by in silico pharmacokinetic modelling (ADMET Predictor®). NiPB is predicted to undergo N-dealkylation, cleavage of the 3,4-methylendioxy moiety, and N-glucuronidation. Computational profiling predicted high BBB permeability, Vd = 4.37 L/kg, fup > 50%, CYP2D6 and OCT2 inhibition, and hERG blockade (pIC50 = 4.888). In vivo, NiPB induced dose-dependent locomotor stimulation without affecting motor coordination and provoked tachypnoea and visual reflex alterations, while tactile and acoustic responses, as well as thermoregulation, were preserved. In conclusion, this study defines the preliminary toxicological profile of NiPB, indicating that acute exposure may trigger central psychostimulant toxicity in vivo. Furthermore, based on the in silico profiling, targeted experimental studies are required to determine the actual cardiotoxicity and risks of drug–drug interactions associated with NiPB.

1. Introduction

Synthetic cathinones are part of the ever-increasing and constantly evolving group of novel psychoactive substances (NPSs)—drugs developed to circumvent legal restrictions on traditional drugs of abuse. The common mechanism of action of synthetic cathinones involves increasing synaptic concentrations of monoamines through interactions with reuptake transporters, triggering effects similar to those of cocaine or amphetamine, such as euphoria, increased sociability, increased energy, reduced fatigue, and intensification of sensory experiences. Conversely, consumers and case reports describe side effects including agitation and aggressiveness, paranoia, psychosis, and hallucinations, alongside cardiovascular complications (tachycardia, thoracic pain, hypertension, cardiac arrest), respiratory distress, hyperthermia, nausea, and vomiting [1].

The emergence and abuse of novel cathinone derivatives have surged in recent years. Worldwide, 228 synthetic cathinones have been reported, with 115 compounds identified between 2024 and 2025 [2]. In 2024, seven new derivatives were first discovered in Europe [3]. In the same year, a novel compound, N-isopropylbutylone (NiPB; Figure 1), was identified alongside methamphetamine in a drug material [4]. This compound has also been found in ecstasy tablets along with methamphetamine and ketamine [5], while its seizure by Italian Authorities was reported in 2025. Structurally, NiPB is closely related to butylone and eutylone (Figure 1), two hybrid transporter compounds that inhibit DAT and NET while possessing substrate-type releasing effects at SERT [6].

In particular, NiPB shares the same 3,4-methylenedioxy ring substitution and α-carbon side chain with eutylone and butylone. Starting from the structure of butylone, the N-alkyl moiety has been sequentially expanded from an N-methyl group (butylone) to an N-ethyl group (eutylone) and then to an N-isopropyl group (NiPB). The increase in the size and bulkiness of the substituent at the amine group is generally associated with an enhanced potency of inhibition at DAT and a significant increase in the DAT/SERT ratio [7]. In line with this, in vitro studies show that butylone and eutylone differ in their DAT inhibitory potency, with reported IC50 values of 1710 ± 320 nM and 120 ± 10 nM, respectively [6,8]. Based on these SAR principles, we hypothesized that the bulky N-isopropyl substitution in NiPB further reinforces DAT inhibitory potency and DAT/SERT selectivity, resulting in a predominantly dopaminergic psychostimulant profile in vivo.

Although a monograph on NiPB was published by the Center for Forensic Science Research and Education [4], data regarding its pharmacological profile and effects in animals or humans remain scarce. To address this critical knowledge gap, our study aims to provide a preliminary evaluation of the pharmaco-toxicological profile of NiPB. In particular, we conducted tests on its ADMET profile using the in silico ADMET Predictor® 14.0 (x64) software and evaluated its acute effects in mice. As a Collaborative Centre of the Department of Anti-Drug Policies (DPA), Presidency of the Council of Ministers (PCM), our objective is to provide relevant toxicological and clinical data to assist forensic experts and clinicians in the management of potential NiPB intoxication cases and to pre-empt a potential health risk associated with the circulation of this compound.

2. Results

2.1. Predicted Metabolic Pathway

Based on ADMET Predictor®, NiPB is estimated to be a substrate of CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP2D6 (Figure 2).

In particular, these enzymes were predicted to promote (i) hydroxylation at the N-isopropyl function and consequently N-dealkylation; (ii) hydroxylation at the 3,4-methylenedioxy moiety, followed by the opening of the ring and production of the 3,4-catechol metabolite, which is predicted to undergo oxidation at the hydroxyl groups. Moreover, UGT1A4 and UGT2B7 were predicted to take part in the metabolism of NiPB, which would produce the N-glucuronic metabolite (Figure 2).

2.2. Predicted ADMET Properties

Table 1 shows the predicted inhibition of cytochrome enzymes by NiPB. Among all the tested CYPs, the compound was predicted to inhibit CYP2D6.

ADMET Predictor® calculated a high penetrance of the blood–brain barrier (BBB; Table 2). NiPB was not predicted to be a substrate or an inhibitor of P-glycoprotein (PgP) and organic cation transporter 1 (OCT1). In contrast, the compound was estimated to be both a substrate and an inhibitor of organic cation transporter 2 (OCT2). The software predicted a good percentage of compound unbound to blood plasma proteins (>50%) in both humans (hum_fup) and mice (mou_fup), and a high volume of distribution at steady state (>3.7 L/kg). Finally, NiPB was not predicted to inhibit BSEP, as the calculated IC50 (BSEP_IC50) value exceeded the threshold of 60 μM.

The toxic potential of NiPB is shown in Table 3. The compound was not predicted to induce alterations in the serum levels of alkaline phosphatase (Ser_AlkPhos), gamma-glutamyl transferase (Ser_GGT), lactate dehydrogenase (Ser_LDH), aspartic acid transaminase (Ser_AST), or alanine transaminase (Ser_ALT). Furthermore, the compound was not predicted to exhibit androgen (Andro_Filter) or estrogen (Estro_Filter) receptor toxicity in rats. Instead, it was predicted to cause respiratory allergenic sensitization in rats (Sens_Resp) and to block the potassium channel in humans (hERG_Filter), with a calculated pIC50 of 4.888.

2.3. Acute Effects in Mice

2.3.1. Physiological Parameters

Systemic injection of the lowest dose of NiPB (0.1 mg/kg) did not induce significant effects in male mice. In contrast, a transient increase in respiration rate was observed at doses of 1 mg/kg (only at 5 min post-administration), 10 mg/kg (until 30 min post-administration), 30 mg/kg (at 5 min and again between 60 and 120 min post-administration), and 60 mg/kg (until 120 min post-treatment) [Figure 3A; two-way RM ANOVA, main effect of treatment: F(5, 30) = 5.131 and p = 0.0016; time: F(7, 210) = 11.02 and p < 0.0001; treatment × time interaction: F(35, 210) = 2.628 and p < 0.0001].

Notably, none of the tested doses of NiPB altered the core body temperature of the mice (Figure 3B).

2.3.2. Sensorial Responses

NiPB induced a significant reduction in the visual placing reflex in male mice. Specifically, the 1 mg/kg dose induced a transient effect, while higher doses (10–60 mg/kg) led to more profound and prolonged impairment [Figure 4A; two-way RM ANOVA, main effect of treatment: F(5, 30) = 114.5 and p < 0.0001, time: F(7, 210) = 60.91 and p < 0.0001, treatment × time interaction: F(35, 210) = 9.155 and p < 0.0001].

However, NiPB (0.1–60 mg/kg) did not affect visual object (Figure 4B), acoustic (Figure 4C), or tactile responses (Figure 4D).

2.3.3. Locomotory Activity

Treatment with NiPB (1–60 mg/kg) induced a dose-dependent increase in spontaneous locomotory activity. Specifically, the 1 and 10 mg/kg doses caused significant effects only during the first 5 and 30 min, respectively. The 30 mg/kg dose increased activity during the first hour and again at 300 min. The highest dose tested induced a persistent stimulatory effect [Figure 5A; two-way RM ANOVA, main effect of treatment: F(5, 30) = 21.74 and p < 0.0001, time: F(7, 210) = 49.66 and p < 0.0001, treatment × time interaction: F(35, 210) = 6.027 and p < 0.0001].

Finally, the compound did not induce motor impairments or affect performance in the rotarod test (Figure 5B).

3. Discussion

The present work provides novel information on a recently identified synthetic cathinone, i.e., NiPB. Given the absence of data on its pharmacokinetic characteristics and its pharmaco-toxicological effects, we evaluated its ADMET properties and its acute effects in male CD-1 mice.

The in silico analysis revealed a metabolic profile consistent with previous computational, in vitro, and in vivo studies on related cathinones [9,10,11,12,13,14]. Indeed, NiPB was predicted to undergo N-dealkylation, producing a metabolite shared with butylone and N-propylbutylone. A second predicted metabolite results from cleavage of the 3,4-methylendioxy moiety. These reactions were predicted to be mediated by CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP2D6. Furthermore, in silico modelling suggested a potential for CYP2D6 inhibition, although this output was generated with moderate prediction confidence (accuracy of 58%), representing a hypothetical risk for pharmacokinetic drug–drug interactions that requires experimental validation. While future studies are needed to confirm these pathways, khat has been reported to inhibit CYP2D6 in humans [15], and an in vitro study demonstrated the ability of methylenedioxy-derived designer drugs, butylone and MDPV, to inhibit this isoform [16]. Furthermore, eutylone was recently shown to be metabolized by CYP2D6, CYP2C19, and CYP2B6 while inducing a time-dependent inhibition of CYP2D6 [17]. Finally, the software predicted phase II N-glucuronidation by UGT1A4 and UGT2B7. Although information regarding phase II metabolites of synthetic cathinones remains limited, glucuronide conjugates have been identified for both eutylone and mephedrone [11,17,18].

Based on our analysis, NiPB exhibits high predicted permeability across the BBB. Additionally, the software suggested a potential interaction with OCT2 as both a substrate and an inhibitor, albeit with modest prediction confidence (accuracies of 67% and 55%, respectively). Given the pivotal role of this transporter in the renal secretion of organic cations [19], this result suggests a theoretical risk for drug–drug interactions that warrants experimental validation. Our computational profiling yielded a predicted human Vd of 4.371 L/kg (slightly above the threshold of 3.7 L/kg), along with a high fraction of compound unbound to plasma proteins (>50%). These parameters are closely interconnected [20]: while the high unbound fraction suggests that a major portion of circulating NiPB potentially remains available for biological interaction, the Vd value points towards a possible propensity for extravascular tissue redistribution in humans, without necessarily implying excessive tissue sequestration. The Vd of synthetic cathinones is a PK parameter influenced by multiple factors, including chemical structure, chirality, dose, and biological sex. For instance, methylone and butylone exhibit greater tissue distribution than pentylone [21], whereas the Vd of MDPV enantiomers shows sex-dependent variations [22]. Furthermore, alpha-PVP has also been reported to possess a high Vd in male rats, highlighting how structural modifications across this substance class affect tissue partitioning profiles [23].

We also evaluated the potential inhibition of BSEP, a crucial hepatic transporter, whose blockade is closely linked to drug-induced liver injury [24]. Similar to MDPV and MDPHP [10], NiPB was not predicted to inhibit BSEP. Furthermore, computational modelling disclosed that NiPB lacks significant propensity for human hepatotoxicity or androgen- or estrogen receptor-mediated toxicity in rat models. Nevertheless, in light of its predicted Vd and potential for tissue redistribution, these toxicological profiles warrant experimental validation in animal models. Indeed, tissue retention and redistribution of drugs of abuse can prolong systemic effects via gradual release back into the bloodstream or induce localized organ toxicity [20]. This is particularly relevant given that synthetic cathinones are frequently associated with multi-organ toxicities, including rhabdomyolysis, hepatotoxicity, and cardiotoxicity [25,26,27,28,29,30]. Finally, NiPB was predicted to act as a respiratory sensitizer. Since synthetic cathinones are commonly administered via the nasal route, their potential to trigger airway hypersensitivity represents a clinically relevant feature [31].

Notably, the compound was predicted to interact with the human hERG potassium channel (pIC50 of 4.888, corresponding to an IC50 of approximately 12.9 μM), indicating a potential risk of QT-interval prolongation and fatal arrhythmias, such as torsades de pointes [32]. In absolute terms, this micromolar affinity indicates a low intrinsic blocking potency at the hERG channel [33]. However, this risk must be contextualized with systemic exposure and free plasma concentrations [34]. While high-dose regimens (up to 60 mg/kg) were evaluated in our behavioural protocol and computational ADMET profiling predicted an unbound fraction exceeding 50%, no systemic pharmacokinetic (PK) data are currently available to measure actual free plasma concentrations in vivo. Therefore, this finding requires experimental confirmation, including dedicated PK evaluations and functional electrophysiological assays, in order to establish the true cardiac safety margin. Cardiotoxicity is among the most frequently reported symptoms of synthetic cathinone intoxications [35], and previous studies have focused on the effects of synthetic cathinones on cardiac function. For example, MDPV was found to induce ventricular bradycardia and AV block in zebrafish model [36] and to prolong the field potential duration in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes [35], which highlights an association between MDPV and QT prolongation. Another example is represented by the atypical synthetic cathinone 4,4′-DMAR, which has recently been demonstrated to induce QT-interval prolongation in male mice [37]. On this basis, future research must prioritize the evaluation of NiPB effects on cardiovascular and cardiomyocyte functions.

As previously mentioned, the circulation of NiPB on the NPS market has only recently been reported; hence, this is the first study to describe its pharmacological effects in mice. Given its chemical structure, NiPB was expected to induce behavioural, physiological, and sensorimotor profiles similar to those previously observed with other synthetic cathinones, particularly 3,4-methylenedioxy derivatives (e.g., eutylone, butylone, MDPV, MDPHP, N-ethylpentylone, dimethylone, and dibutylone) [6,8,10,38]. In accordance with this hypothesis, NiPB induced dose-dependent locomotor stimulation and transient tachypnoea while inhibiting the visual placing response, which points toward an alteration in proprioceptive reflex control. The compound did not affect other sensorimotor responses or motor coordination. This contrasts with other psychoactive substances associated with disrupted acoustic or tactile reactivity, such as NM2AI or MTTA [39,40], or with marked stereotypies and postural instability, such as MDPV, 3-FMC, 4-FMC, or 3-CMC [10,25,41]. Furthermore, NiPB did not alter thermoregulation in mice. While this differs from the hyperthermic responses frequently reported following cathinone consumption in humans [42], it aligns with the modest, if any, effects on rodent body temperature observed with several related compounds [43,44].

Based on previous observations with related synthetic cathinones, we anticipated significant locomotor stimulation even at low doses of NiPB. For instance, Glatfelter and colleagues [6] showed that eutylone produces significant hyperlocomotion in male C57BL/6J mice at a dose of 3 mg/kg (s.c.). Similarly, our previous work [10] with CD-1 mice demonstrated that MDPV increases the total distance travelled at 1 mg/kg (i.p.). In contrast, NiPB exhibited lower in vivo potency, as significant locomotor activation was observed only at higher doses (10–60 mg/kg). From a structure–activity relationship (SAR) perspective [7], we initially hypothesized that NiPB would possess higher dopamine transporter (DAT) inhibitory potency than eutylone, ultimately producing greater locomotor activation. However, Glatfelter et al. (2021) demonstrated that, despite differences in α-carbon and amine side-chain substituents, eutylone, pentylone, and dibutylone display comparable DAT interactions while exhibiting distinct potencies in stimulating locomotion [6]. This underscores that in vitro SAR data do not always directly correlate with in vivo behavioural outcomes. Nevertheless, our findings demonstrate for the first time that NiPB acts as a psychostimulant, aligning with the general profile of synthetic cathinones.

Because direct in vitro binding or functional assays of monoamine transporters were not performed in the present study, the exact neurochemical mechanism underlying the actions of NiPB remains to be established. Nevertheless, the observed behavioural and physiological responses are broadly consistent with monoaminergic activation. In particular, central noradrenergic pathways are known to regulate respiratory rhythm via α-adrenergic receptors in the brainstem [45,46,47] and to modulate sensorimotor reflex integration such as vestibulo-ocular and optokinetic responses [48], providing a plausible functional context for the observed tachypnoea and visual placing impairment. This observation aligns with reported data for eutylone and butylone, which display NET inhibitory potencies of 1280 ± 140 nM and 920 ± 130 nM, respectively [6,8]. Similarly, dose-dependent hyperlocomotion represents a characteristic behavioural signature often associated with increased synaptic DA levels in the ventral striatum [7], consistent with the known effects of reference cathinones and other psychostimulants [49,50,51]. Regarding central nervous system (CNS) accessibility, the observed dose-dependent behavioural effects support central activity and are consistent with the in silico predictions of high BBB permeability.

Finally, related cathinones such as eutylone (IC50 = 690 ± 50 nM and EC50 = 1020 ± 260 nM) and butylone (IC50 = 680 ± 130 nM) [6,8] display SERT activity, which in vivo is frequently associated with hyperthermia and disruptions of tactile or acoustic reflexes, as described for serotonergic psychostimulants like MTTA, NM2AI, or 4,4′-DMAR [39,40,52]. In our study, the tested dose range of NiPB failed to induce these characteristic serotoninergic signs. However, the absence of these manifestations cannot be interpreted as proof of DAT/SERT selectivity of preferential dopaminergic/noradrenergic activation. Direct in vitro binding and functional reuptake/release assays remain strictly necessary to definitively characterize the target affinity, selectivity profile, and transporter interactions of NiPB.

4. Materials and Methods

4.1. ADMET Prediction

Simulation Plus ADMET Predictor® Version 10.4 (x64) on a Windows 11 operating system (ADMET Predictor® 14.0, Simulations-Plus Inc., Durham, NC, USA) was employed to predict the ADMET profile of NiPB. As mentioned in previous studies [10,25,53], this cheminformatics platform utilizes Quantitative Structure–Activity/Property Relationship (QSAR/QSPR) machine learning models, primarily Artificial Neural Network Ensembles (ANNE), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Kernel Partial Least Squares (KPLS), trained on curated experimental datasets of well-defined drugs using 2D molecular structures and atomic descriptors. Unlike platforms relying on static literature lookup tables or basic web utilities, ADMET Predictor® employs ensemble architectures to maintain predictive performance when applied to novel chemical structures. Model robustness and generalizability are ensured by partitioning datasets into training, verification, and external test sets (via Kohonen self-organizing maps or stratified sampling) alongside early stopping protocols to prevent overtraining. Predictive performance is validated using held-out external test sets assessed using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and R2 for continuous properties, as well as Concordance (accuracy), Sensitivity, and Specificity for classification models. In independent comparative evaluations, ADMET Predictor®’s physicochemical models (e.g., S + logP and S + Sw) have demonstrated superior or comparable performance relative to other widely used prediction platforms (e.g., Dragon) and established literature QSAR models. Furthermore, to prevent overconfident extrapolation, all predictions incorporate defined applicability domain assessments and generate compound-specific confidence metrics.

4.2. Animals

Thirty-six adult male ICR (CD-1®) mice (3–4 months old, weighing 25–30 g; ENVIGO Harlan Italy, Ferrara, Italy; bred inside the Laboratory for Preclinical Research (LARP) of University of Ferrara, Italy), were group-housed (5 mice per cage; a floor area per animal of 80 cm2; a minimum enclosure height of 12 cm). Animals were exposed to a 12:12-h light–dark cycle at a temperature of 20–22 °C and humidity of 45–55%, with ad libitum access to food (Diet 4RF25 GLP; Mucedola, Settimo Milanese, Milan, Italy) and water. The experimental protocols followed in the present study were in accordance with the U.K. Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act of 1986 and associated guidelines and the new European Communities Council Directive of September 2010 (2010/63/EU). The Italian Ministry of Health (license no. 1168/2024-PR, CBCC2.79.EXT.44) and the Animal Welfare Body of the University of Ferrara approved experimental protocols. According to the ARRIVE guidelines, all possible efforts were made to minimize the number of animals used and the animals’ pain and discomfort. For the present study, 6 mice were employed for each treatment (vehicle or 5 different doses of NiPB, 0.1–60 mg/kg). An a priori power analysis was performed using G*Power 3.1 [54] to determine the total sample size for the behavioural testing protocol. Based on the expected dose-dependent pharmacological profiles (effect size f calculated according to Cohen, 1988 [55]), a significance level of α = 0.05, and a statistical power of 1–β = 0.80, a sample size of 6 animals per group was calculated to be sufficient to detect an effect size of 0.50 for the primary behavioural endpoint (tactile reflex). The GraphPad calculator [56] was employed to randomly assign subjects to treatment groups. We randomly assigned a total of 6 subjects to each of the 6 groups.

4.3. Drug Preparation and Dose Selection

N-isopropylbutylone hydrochloride was purchased from LGC Standards S.r.l. (Milan, Italy). The compound was dissolved in saline solution (0.9% NaCl), which was also employed as the vehicle. The drug was administered via intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection at a volume of 4 µL/g. The doses of the tested compound were chosen based on previous studies conducted with synthetic cathinones (MDPV and MDPHP) and a cathinone-like compound (MTTA) [10,39].

4.4. Behavioural Studies

For the present study, the effects of systemic administration of NiPB at different doses on behavioural responses were investigated as previously described [25,40] using a battery of tests largely employed in our laboratory for Safety Pharmacology studies in a murine model [57]. The protocol was designed to minimize the number of mice employed and consisted of consecutive functional observational tests, according to the following scheme: respiratory rate, spontaneous locomotion, sensorimotor (visual placing, visual object, acoustic, and overall tactile) reflexes, rectal temperature, and stimulated motor activity. The battery of tests was conducted at 0 (basal values), 5, 30, 60, 120, 180, 240, and 300 min after treatment with vehicle or NiPB (0.1–60 mg/kg). During the experiment, mice were individually housed in an experimental chamber (350 mm × 350 mm × 350 mm) with black methacrylate walls and a transparent front door. The randomized assignment of each subject to a treatment group (see Section 4.2) and the drug preparation (see Section 4.3) were conducted by a single operator, while behavioural observations were conducted by different trained operators working in pairs who were not aware of the treatment.

4.4.1. Respiratory Rate

To assess respiratory rate, mice were placed in individual cages and allowed to move freely [25]. An operator analyzed video footage of the mice’s videotaped respiration patterns offline and counted the number of the animal’s thoracic extensions within a minute.

4.4.2. Mobility Time

The mobility time test involved allowing the animal to move freely in a square plastic cage (60 cm × 60 cm) and using a stopwatch to measure the total time the animal remained in motion over a period of 300 s (5 min) [40]. Mouse activity was recorded using one camera (B/W USB day and night with varifocal, Ugo Basile, Ferrara, Italy), and the recordings were analyzed offline in a blind manner by a different operator.

4.4.3. Visual Responses

To evaluate the ability of the animal to capture visual information, two different tests were performed: one when the animal was stationary (visual object) and the other when the animal was moving (visual placing) [40].

The visual placing test was performed using a modified tail-suspension apparatus that brought the mouse toward the floor at a constant speed of 10 cm/sec. Analysis of the video frames made it possible to evaluate the start of the mouse’s reaction as it approached the floor. Mice typically respond by extending the front paws, and an electronic ruler measures the perpendicular distance (mm) from the floor at which the mouse starts the reaction.

The visual object test was performed to evaluate the mice’s ability to respond to the sight of an approaching object presented from the front (using a white horizontal bar) or from the side (using a small dentist’s mirror). A score of 1 was assigned if the mouse showed a response to the stimulus, and a score of 0 if no response was observed. Mice usually respond by turning their head or retracting. For the frontal visual response, the bar was moved toward the front of the mouse’s head 3 times. For the lateral visual response, the procedure was conducted bilaterally and repeated 3 times. The total score was calculated by summing the scores obtained from each test (overall score: 9).

4.4.4. Acoustic Responses

In the acoustic test, four different stimuli (varying in intensity and frequency) were presented behind the animal, and the reflex response of the mouse was recorded by the operator [25]. Each stimulus was repeated 3 times, with a score of 1 in the presence of a reflex or 0 if absent. The total score was calculated by summing the scores obtained from each test (overall score: 12).

4.4.5. Tactile Responses

The tactile responses of mice were assessed through vibrissae, corneal, and pinnae reflexes [40] using a gavage needle, with a score of 1 in the presence of a response or 0 if absent. Reflexes were assessed by gently touching the vibrissae (right and left, once per side), the cornea (right and left, 3 times per side), and pinnae (left and right, 2 times per side). Data are expressed as the sum of the three parameters (overall score: 12).

4.4.6. Body Temperature

Core temperature was evaluated using a probe (1 mm diameter) connected to a Cole–Parmer digital thermometer (model 8402; Vernon Hills, IL, USA). After lubrication with liquid vaseline, the probe was gently inserted into the rectum of the mouse (to a depth of approximately 2 cm) and left in position until the temperature stabilized (approximately 10 s) [25].

4.4.7. Rotarod

The accelerod test was used to assess alterations in stimulated motor activity induced by NiPB [25]. Mice were placed on the rotarod, which consists of a rotating cylinder that constantly increases its rotation speed (0–60 rotations/min over 5 min). The time for which mice could stand on the rotarod during a period of 300 s was measured using a stopwatch.

4.5. Data and Statistical Analysis

Data are represented as % of basal values (respiratory rate, visual placing response, mobility time, and rotarod), as Δ°C relative to basal values (rectal temperature), and as arbitrary units (visual object, acoustic, and overall tactile responses). All data are shown as mean ± SEM from 6 independent experimental replications. The Shapiro–Wilk test was used to establish and confirm the normality of the parameters. Two-way RM ANOVA followed by Bonferroni’s test for multiple comparisons was employed for the statistical analysis of the effects of NiPB (0.1–60 mg/kg; i.p.) over time. All statistical analyses were performed using Prism 8.0 software (GraphPad Prism, San Diego, CA, USA). Results were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05 (solid symbol) versus vehicle.

5. Conclusions and Real-World Implications

The present work addresses a critical gap in the literature regarding NiPB, a novel synthetic cathinone that, although not yet associated with documented clinical intoxication, poses an emerging threat as illicit markets adapt to legislative restrictions on structural predecessors [58]. Identifying new compounds and establishing appropriate diagnostic methods, clinical management, and treatment protocols for cases of novel psychoactive substance (NPS)-related intoxication remains a significant challenge [59].

Although limited to acute observations in male mice and computational modelling, our findings offer preliminary insights into the potential risk profile of NiPB, particularly in scenarios involving acute overdose or polydrug use. The in silico ADMET profiling predicted potential hERG channel blockage, generating a theoretical hypothesis regarding cardiotoxicity. While cardiovascular symptoms such as tachycardia, palpitations, and chest pain, potentially escalating to cardiac arrest, myocardial infarction, and life-threatening arrhythmias, are well documented for the cathinone-containing plant khat [60] and related synthetic cathinones [61,62,63], dedicated assays and exposure measurements are required to evaluate whether NiPB exerts direct cardiotoxic effects in vivo.

Another critical aspect emerging from clinical case reports is the occurrence of severe agitation, aggressiveness, and acute psychosis among synthetic cathinone users [25,61,62,64]. From a translational perspective, drug-induced hyperlocomotion in rodents provides a preclinical parallel to psychomotor agitation. This characteristic response to acute synthetic cathinone intoxication [41] presents a major challenge in emergency settings, as severe agitation hampers patient management and clinical examination and complicates the collection of information regarding the ingested substance and dosage. In this regard, the dose-dependent hyperlocomotion observed in mice after treatment with NiPB suggests that the compound could potentially be associated with similar behavioural manifestations following acute exposure.

Synthetic cathinones are frequently co-consumed with other illicit substances, including alcohol, cannabis, and stimulant-like compounds [65], as well as sedatives and opioids [66,67]. Moreover, users are often unaware of multi-substance exposure, as commercial “bath salt” products frequently contain undisclosed mixtures, and NPS may be added as adulterants or cutting agents [66,68,69]. Our in silico evaluation suggests that NiPB might inhibit CYP2D6 and OCT2, generating a preliminary hypothesis regarding drug–drug interactions. If experimentally validated, such inhibition could alter the clearance of co-administered substances, potentially increasing the risk of systemic toxicity.

Finally, while human biotransformation profiles remain to be fully characterized, recent in vivo evidence in mice [70] supports the predicted metabolic pathways, offering a baseline for analytical screening protocols in forensic and clinical toxicology. In this framework, integrating computational ADMET profiling with in vivo screening offers a rapid, cost-effective, and ethically sound strategy to proactively characterize newly emerging NPS before widespread clinical presentation occurs.

6. Limitations

Several methodological limitations of the present study should be noted. While computational modelling successfully predicted central penetration, in silico predictions require full in vitro and in vivo validation. Specifically, formal radioligand-binding and functional transporter assays are needed to definitively quantify the affinity and selectivity of NiPB at DAT, NET, and SERT. The absence of systemic PK measurements in the present study precludes a direct correlation between circulating plasma exposure and the observed behavioural or physiological effects. Moreover, in vivo testing was restricted to male subjects, a choice aligned with the higher epidemiological prevalence of synthetic cathinone use among males [71]. However, given that synthetic cathinones are also consumed by females [72] and that sex can markedly influence psychostimulant pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics [25,44,73,74,75], future investigations should prioritize evaluating sex-tailored responses, full internal PK profiling, and direct electrophysiological assessments of cardiac safety.

Simple Summary

Sled dogs have been essential to life in the Arctic for centuries, helping people travel, hunt, and transport goods across challenging environments. Although they are often viewed as working animals and cultural symbols, their role as a form of technology has received less attention. This article explores how sled dogs can be understood as living technologies that developed through long-term relationships between humans and animals. We argue that transportation may have been one of the earliest and most important reasons for the development of the human dog partnership. As people moved across northern landscapes, dogs that could assist with carrying resources and pulling loads may have provided a significant advantage, creating strong incentives for continued cooperation, breeding, and training. Over many generations, these practices produced animals with physical and behavioural traits suited to endurance, mobility, and collaborative work. Together with sleds, harnesses, and travel knowledge, sled dogs formed integrated transportation systems that enabled human movement and survival in Arctic environments. By examining these relationships through the lens of technology, this article shows how domestication was not only a biological process but also a technological one, shaped by the co-development of humans, animals, and transport systems over thousands of years.

Abstract

In recent years, the intersection of the history of technology, environmental history, and ethnozoology has generated new insights into human–animal relationships, particularly in Arctic contexts where survival has depended on close interspecies collaboration. Sled dogs, which have long played a central role in Arctic lifeways, exemplify how animals function as active participants in socio-ecological systems and can be understood as forms of biological technology. Through domestication, selective breeding, and sustained practices of training and care, sled dogs developed physiological, behavioural, and genetic traits associated with endurance, thermoregulation, metabolism, and cooperative work. At the same time, humans developed harnesses, sleds, and mobility practices designed to work in tandem with canine capabilities, forming integrated transportation systems. Building on this perspective, we propose a transportation hypothesis of dog domestication. Rather than viewing transport as a late application of already domesticated dogs, we argue that mobility may have been one of the principal technological functions through which the human–dog partnership became evolutionarily and culturally stable. Under this framework, domestication is understood not only as a biological process but also as a technological one, shaped through the co-development of animals, transport systems, and human knowledge. This perspective broadens technological and ethnozoological inquiry and highlights the role of domestication and cross-cultural knowledge in Arctic human–animal relationships.

1. Introduction

The relationship between humans and dogs represents one of the oldest and most influential technological partnerships in human history. Since the Late Pleistocene, dogs have accompanied people as hunters, companions, guards, and transport animals, enabling humans to occupy environments that would otherwise have been difficult to exploit [1,2,3,4]. Nowhere is this relationship more evident than in the Arctic, where the collaboration between humans and dogs has shaped patterns of mobility, subsistence, exploration, and cultural development for millennia.

Mobility has long been a defining challenge of Arctic life. Vast distances, highly seasonal resources, and extreme environmental conditions demanded efficient systems for transporting people, food, equipment, and materials across snow and sea ice. Archaeological discoveries from the Zhokhov site in the New Siberian Islands, including sled components and dog remains dating to approximately 9000 years ago, demonstrate that dogs were already functioning as draft animals during the Early Holocene [5,6]. Since then, dog sledding has become one of the most enduring technological systems of the circumpolar North. Dogs facilitated hunting, trade, communication, and travel across otherwise inaccessible landscapes for the ancestors of indigenous populations or Arctic North America, the Inuit, Yu’pik, and Aleuts. They later enabled some of the most significant Arctic and Antarctic expeditions, including Knud Rasmussen’s Fifth Thule Expedition, the Denmark Expedition led by Ludvig Mylius-Erichsen, and Roald Amundsen’s successful journey to the South Pole [7,8].

Despite their historical importance, sled dog populations have declined substantially in recent decades. In Greenland alone, the registered sled dog population decreased from approximately 25,000 animals in 2002 to around 15,000 by 2016, with numbers continuing to decline due to climate change, diminishing sea ice, socioeconomic transformation, and reduced reliance on subsistence hunting [9]. This decline threatens not only a distinctive dog population but also one of the world’s oldest continuously operating human–animal technological systems. Beyond their archaeological and cultural significance, these findings have important conservation and welfare implications. Protecting sled dog health, genetic diversity, and working conditions is essential for sustaining both animal welfare and the cultural heritage embedded in Arctic human–dog relationships. Continued population declines may therefore have consequences that extend beyond the dogs themselves to the preservation of Indigenous knowledge, traditional husbandry practices, and the long-term viability of one of the world’s oldest human–animal working partnerships [9]. However, there are ongoing local initiatives that aim to protect the endangered Greenlandic sled dog and its cultural heritage through year-round sustainable tourism, hands-on visitor education, and local breeding traditions.

Traditionally, technology has been associated with mechanical inventions and industrial development. Such perspectives have tended to separate technology from nature, reinforcing the assumption that technologies are necessarily manufactured, inert objects [10,11]. Yet throughout human history, many of the most transformative technologies have been living. Domesticated plants and animals have fundamentally altered human societies through agriculture, transport, communication, and labour. The domestication and selective breeding of animals therefore constitute technological practices in their own right, producing living systems whose biological characteristics have been shaped through sustained human intervention [12,13,14].

Sled dogs exemplify this relationship between biology and technology. A dog team is more than a collection of animals pulling a sled; it is an integrated technological system in which humans, dogs, harnesses, sleds, and the environment operate together. The effectiveness of this system depends upon continual communication, cooperation, and mutual adaptation. Commands, body position, terrain, weather, and the responses of individual dogs all contribute to a dynamic process in which technology is enacted through movement rather than simply embodied in an artefact. The musher and the dogs function as a coordinated technological unit, blurring conventional distinctions between operator and tool, nature and technology [15,16].

Viewing sled dogs as living technologies also invites a reconsideration of domestication itself. Existing models of dog domestication have primarily emphasized commensal scavenging, hunting partnerships, or social companionship as the principal selective forces driving the emergence of domestic dogs [17,18]. While these explanations have substantially advanced our understanding of domestication, they pay comparatively little attention to mobility as a technological challenge. If transportation became essential to human survival and expansion in northern environments, it is plausible that the capacity of early dogs to assist with moving people and resources represented one of the earliest sustained selective pressures reinforcing domestication.

Building upon this perspective, we propose a transportation hypothesis of dog domestication. Rather than viewing transport as a relatively late application of already domesticated dogs, we argue that transportation may itself have constituted one of the principal technological functions through which the human–dog partnership became evolutionarily and culturally stable. Under this hypothesis, domestication is understood not solely as a biological or behavioural process, but as a technological one in which selective breeding, training, and increasingly sophisticated transport systems co-evolved over thousands of years.

This article contributes to the history of technology by reframing sled dogs as living technologies and by positioning transportation as a potential driver of dog domestication. Through this approach, we argue that domestication should be understood as both an evolutionary and a technological process, one in which humans and dogs co-created a living system that transformed mobility, enabled Arctic adaptation, and continues to embody a unique form of intangible cultural heritage.

2. Background: The Versatile Role of Dogs in Arctic Societies

Dogs have played an essential and diverse role in many northern communities, especially in Arctic societies [19]. Sled dogs have supported humans in hunting and herding activities and have been widely used for transportation [1,20,21,22]. They also served as food sources, ceremonial offerings, and appear in Inuit cosmology and mythology. Dogs had multiple functions not only during their lives but also after death [21,23]. Archaeological excavations in North America and Siberia have uncovered dog bones with cut marks, indicating they were butchered [24,25]. For example, at the Ust’-Polui site in Siberia, many dog bones show signs of slaughter [25]. Dog remains were also used as raw materials, such as for clothing [26]. Sled dogs have a thick, three-layered coat that allowed them to survive Arctic conditions, a material that humans used to protect themselves from the cold [26]. We suggest that the technological advance provided by dogs in the form of transportation, through pack, sled, travois, and other mediums, shaped the early dogs during the domestication process in Eurasia.

Sled dogs constitute a distinctive form of living technology, not merely as working animals but as biological actors possessing specific characteristics that makes them essential within Arctic transport mobility systems. Across the circumpolar Arctic, sled dogs have collaborated with humans for more than 9000 years, underscoring both their technological significance and their cultural value [6,27]. Arctic sled dog types, including the Siberian Husky, Alaskan Malamute, Canadian Inuit Dog, and the Greenlandic sled dog (Qimmeq), share close common ancestors but have developed specialized adaptations to the Arctic and sledding performance [27,28]. The Greenlandic sled dog is of particular interest, as this population has retained its functional role as a sled dog in Greenland for nearly a millennium, without the extensive intervention or transformation into companion animals that other Arctic breeds have undergone [28]. In fact the migrations of humans can be traced through the ancestry of dogs in the Arctic, underscoring their role within the suite of tools of arctic societies [1,27,28,29]. Genetics have established that the genetic ancestry that defines sled dogs genetically was present in Siberia already 9700 years ago as evidenced by the genome of a dog originating from Khatystyr cave in Southeast Siberia [30]. It has also been suggested that thermal reception, an Arctic key evolutionary trait [31,32], was already under selection in the dogs, as well as hypoxia adaptation, likely related to the extreme athletic performance of the dogs during sledding as seen in the Zhokhov dog genome [27]. Together this suggests that by the early Holocene the sled dog lineage that continues today was already specialised for sledding and Arctic conditions. Interestingly, the modern sled dogs show genetic adaptation to a diet rich in fatty acids [27], likely a result of humans feeding them marine mammal blubber over generations. However, these mechanisms are not evolved in the ancient Zhokhov dog [27], indicating that across time sled dogs have continued to evolve, and as living beings will continue to do so. Greenland is unique in that the Greenland Sled Dog continues to live and work within the Indigenous sledding culture in which it evolved, preserving a human–dog relationship that has persisted since the arrival of the Thule Inuit more than 800 years ago [28]. Amazingly, the adaptation to cope with a diet rich in fatty acids is an ability co-evolved in polar bears [33] and Arctic humans as the Inuit [34,35]. Being a biological example of convergent evolution and further connecting sled dogs and Arctic cultures, they have followed each other for so long that they have evolved in the same direction.

The evolution, ancestry, physiology and behaviour of the sled dog reflect its life across millennia and the living dogs embody all this legacy. These dogs are robust, possessing dense coats, strength, and endurance, and they exhibit social and communicative capacities that enable them to operate within complex teams. Sled dogs acquire skills through practice and socialization within the pack, where hierarchy and cooperation are essential for effective sled travel [22]. These characteristics are not static but develop through ongoing interactions with humans, the landscape, and technological objects such as sleds and harnesses [16].

There is strong archaeological evidence for the use of sled dogs during the Thule period (1200-1850 CE) across the North American Arctic [36]. These dogs originally came from Siberia and spread through the Bering Strait into central and eastern Arctic regions [1]. This movement aligns with the spread of related technologies found in archaeological records [36]. Sled dogs enabled long-distance travel, connected communities, and supported the use of marine resources. European expeditions in the Arctic relied heavily on Inuit knowledge and their use of dogs for transport. In this context, dogs acted as resilient partners and as a bridge between traditional ways of life and new challenges, continuing to support mobility. Throughout historical transitions, the presence or absence of sled dogs shows that they have been active participants in the adaptation of Arctic life ways. By enhancing human capacity to respond to environmental, spatial, and cultural challenges, dogs have played a key role in innovation and change in the Arctic.

Activities such as sledding and hunting integrate dogs’ physical capacities with human planning, tool use, and social organization, including speed, climate resistance, and tracking ability. Together, they form a technology that neither species could achieve alone. This cooperation has enabled Arctic peoples to understand and interact with their environment in new and creative ways. Sled dogs have thus contributed to human development and helped communities adapt to change. They have enabled movement across tundra, ice, and sea, and supported adaptation and resilience in a landscape shaped by constant transformation [16]. The many roles of sled dogs, from transport and hunting to protection, demonstrate their remarkable versatility and adaptability. Their long-standing relationship with humans reflects a mutual domestication process or co-domestication [22,37,38]. This form of coexistence offers insight into the complex and dynamic relationships between humans and animals throughout history and deepens our understanding of how these relationships have shaped both cultural practices and technological systems.

3. Domestication and Living Technologies

The timing, geographical, and cultural context of dog domestication remain debated, although archaeological and genomic evidence increasingly indicates that the process began during the Late Pleistocene in Eurasia [4]. This precedes the appearance of clearly recognisable archaeological dog remains in the early Holocene including the widely accepted Bonn Oberkassel dog dated to approximately 14,000 years ago [39]. Recent ancient genomic studies have demonstrated that dogs were already genetically distinct from wolves by at least approximately 15,800 years ago [2,4] and genomic divergence estimates have placed the separation of the dog lineage from wolves considerably earlier, potentially during the period between approximately 20,000 and 40,000 years ago [40,41,42]. The geographic location of this process remains unresolved, although it is widely accepted that it occurred in Eurasia. Rather than supporting a single, definitively established centre of domestication, the available evidence is therefore consistent with a complex process occurring within Late Pleistocene hunter–gatherer societies, with suggestions of dual domestication [43], early diversification [44], early specialisation [27], and widespread movements of dogs [4,26,30]. Importantly, the substantial chronological gap between the inferred origins of the domestic dog and the evidence for specialised working dogs presents a challenge for determining the mechanisms and motivations that led to the dog lineage.

When wolves were first domesticated, humans had no prior experience with domestication, making it unlikely that they had a clear plan or goal, such as turning wolves into herding dogs. One of the key components in the mystery of the origin of domestic dogs is what could possibly make an efficient reproductive barrier between early dogs and wolves, allowing the common ancestry of all dogs to drift sufficiently away from wolves becoming the clear lineage that dogs represent. Potentially sledding ability could be such a barrier. The authors would like to underline that this idea remain an explicitly limited hypothesis, as no evidence from the actual context of dog domestication can be provided. The transportation hypothesis relies on observations from traditional sled dog breeding, which corroborates that sledding performance is a barrier to admixture with wolves, entertaining the idea of whether similar mechanisms have played a role as a barrier in the past. Traditional knowledge from Inughuaq hunters and mushers in Avanersuaq (North Greenland) with experience in working with wolf–sled dog hybrids explain how the first generation of wolf dog offspring are unable to pull a sled efficiently, due to their body shape, and that several generations of out breeding with dog ancestry is needed to have a “sled dog” with part wolf ancestry [45]. The low utility of hybrids to pull sleds due to their legs being too long is further supported as mentioned in historical anecdotes. Specifically in the context of Greenland sled dogs, where occurrence of wolf hybridization is documented [45,46], it is noteworthy that no Arctic wolf ancestry have been detected in over 100 dogs that have been genome-sequenced and tested [27,28]. Pointing out that, while wolf–dog hybrids do occur, they have not contributed significantly to the overall gene pool of Greenland sled dogs, with the poor sledding performance of hybrids being a possible contributing factor. If early dogs obtained or had adaptations favourable in sledding, that would put a selection pressure on wolf hybrids. In this way sledding could be a bottleneck of reproductive isolation from wolves in the common ancestry of all dogs, a tradition maintained in modern sled dogs, but lost in other dogs as their ancestors diversified into other ways of life across human cultures. Taming is often seen as the first step in the domestication process, but coincidences likely played a major role. Taming changes behaviour, while domestication changes both behaviour and genetics. Domestication represents a continuous process that relies upon the sustained, multigenerational influence over breeding strategies to produce a lineage shaped by the partner organism [17,18]. A likely scenario is that domestication happened gradually through many small, mostly unintentional steps. These changes were driven by immediate, practical needs rather than long-term breeding strategies. One possible starting point was wolves living near human settlements, feeding on waste, like bones and food scraps. Humans may have tolerated, or even appreciated, these wolves, as they helped dispose of waste and could alert people to danger from wild animals or strangers. Genetic research has supported this with the identification of genes under selection in dogs that are associated with starch digestion [47]; however, these adaptations may have followed the onset of the Neolithic when cereals were domesticated [48], which is supported by the absence of these adaptations in Arctic dogs [27]. Wolves that were less fearful of humans had better access to food and were more likely to survive and reproduce. Over time, this led to natural selection favouring less fearful, more human-friendly wolves. Eventually, some of these wolves may have entered human camps and been treated as semi-domesticated animals, providing companionship or serving as food sources. When deciding which animals to kill, humans likely removed the most aggressive ones first. This would have further encouraged willing behaviour in the population. Over generations, these ‘proto-dogs’ began to look and behave very differently from wild wolves and were eventually recognized as the dog. This long-term process led to significant behavioural and physical changes, creating a distinct population.

Although dogs are considered the first domesticated animals, domestication should be viewed as an ongoing process. The relationship between humans and dogs is best described as co-domestication, where both species adapt to each other [22]. To understand this process, it is important to move away from a human-centred view and instead highlight the role of animals in history [48]. In this multispecies perspective, objects often act as mediators between humans and animals. For example, McNiven [15] describes the canoe as a tool that mediates the hunting relationship between humans and marine animals. Other technologies, such as tools or navigation skills, are also key to how northern peoples interact with working animals [37]. In northern societies, domestication often takes place in shared landscapes where humans and animals live together. The interaction between animals, landscapes, tools, and people is essential to understanding domestication. The landscape itself connects species and shapes their relationships [49]. In this ecological system, cooperation between humans and dogs is grounded in the environment. The relationship between animals and technology is mutual. Technologies are not just tools for managing animals; animals and animistic beliefs also help us understand technology.

Thus, as relationships between humans and wolves became more established, additional opportunities for cooperation may have emerged. While hunting is often proposed as one of the earliest functional roles of dogs, transportation represents another possible context for the development of human–dog cooperation. Archaeological evidence for early transport technologies provides tentative support for considering mobility in this context, although it does not by itself demonstrate that dogs were used for traction [6,50]. We propose that use in transportation was an early driving force that propelled the adoption of proto-dogs or wolves into domestic environments that lead to the distinct animals we now know as dogs. Archaeological evidence indicates that sledding technologies were present in the Late Pleistocene; however, even before the invention of formal sled technology, wolves or early dogs may have assisted people by carrying light loads or dragging simple travois, reducing the energetic costs of transporting resources across landscapes that would be challenging to identify in the archaeological record. In highly seasonal northern environments, where mobility was essential for following game and moving camps, even modest assistance with transport would have provided a considerable advantage. Individuals that were more tolerant of human direction, more willing to work cooperatively, and physically capable of pulling loads would have been preferentially retained and reproduced, strengthening selection for behavioural traits associated with domestication. Although direct archaeological evidence for the earliest use of dogs in transport remains scarce, the antiquity and widespread distribution of sled dogs across the Arctic suggest that transportation may have been one of the earliest specialised roles that reinforced and accelerated the domestication process, rather than simply representing a later cultural innovation. Furthermore, the environmental condition present at the time of the divergence of the dog and grey wolf lineages was colder than the present day; as a result conditions supporting sledding would have been more widespread across Eurasia as suggested by palaeoenvironmental reconstructions [51,52,53]. For highly mobile hunter–gatherers, particularly those inhabiting seasonal and resource-variable environments, efficient movement was fundamental to survival. Even before the emergence of sophisticated sleds, early dogs may have assisted by carrying loads or dragging simple transport devices, increasing hunting efficiency, facilitating residential mobility, and expanding the distances over which people could transport food, raw materials, and equipment. Individuals that were more cooperative, tractable, and responsive to human direction would consequently have been preferentially retained and bred. Transportation therefore acted not simply as a use of dogs, but as a technological niche that favoured behavioural and physiological traits associated with domestication itself. In this framework, mobility became a driver of co-evolution [51].

Domestication Through Material Culture

In Arctic human–animal relationships, material culture and environmentally situated practices are often central to the development of shared systems [16]. The ongoing domestication of dogs, specifically sled dogs, involves skill learning by both humans and animals. This mutual learning is essential to the cooperation between sled mushers and their dogs. Acquiring a skill, as required by technology, is a key part of the domestication process. It involves repeated actions and develops over time. Dogs learn to understand verbal and non-verbal communication, procedures, and gestures, while humans learn how to guide and respond to the dogs. Communication between the musher and the dogs often involves harnesses, whips and buckles (Figure 1), not just voice or body language. These tools have been continuously refined for this purpose. Therefore, technical learning must be mutual and based on shared experience and cooperation, not just imposed on the animal [38].

Objects like dog whips and harnesses can be seen as tools through which humans can communicate their intention to the dogs (Figure 1). When considering how dogs and humans interact physically, harnesses in particular bring the two species into contact and signal the next step, such as preparing the dog for sledding. These tools also create a framework for domestication and act as social infrastructures. If seen only as instruments of human control, they fail to support communication in a shared landscape of coexistence. Becoming a working animal involves many factors, including the physical environment, the nature of the landscape, and the practical knowledge held by both experienced mushers and dogs.

4. Animals as Technological Agents

To understand sled dogs as part of the history of technology, we must consider what kind of system they are part of. In the Arctic, the sled dog system can be seen as a network that includes dogs, humans, sleds, harnesses, feeding strategies, and breeding practices. Together, these elements form an integrated system that enables transportation and survival in extreme environments. Approaches like Actor-Network Theory (ANT) [54,55] and Human–Animal Studies (HAS) offer useful frameworks for analysing such systems. These perspectives discuss humans, animals, and tools as interconnected actors that influence and shape one another.

Sled dogs are not passive tools in a technological system; instead, they are co-actors with a degree of autonomy and unpredictability. This view aligns with recent work in environmental history and multispecies studies, which emphasize the dynamic and reciprocal nature of human–animal relationships [56]. The idea that animals can be part of technological systems has gained attention in the history of technology and multispecies research. These fields challenge the traditional view of technology as only non-living, human-made objects. Instead, they propose a broader definition that includes living beings, such as domesticated, trained, or bred animals, as technological components [10,13]. Some scholars argue that animals like sled dogs can be seen as biotechnological agents, functioning within infrastructures and production systems alongside machines and tools [57]. Others, especially in posthumanism and multispecies studies, caution against reducing animals to mere tools. They emphasize the agency of animals and argue that technological relationships should be understood as mutual and context-dependent [56,58]. Using ANT and HAS allows for a more nuanced analysis of sled dogs as technology. This includes their biological abilities, social roles, and interactions with material tools. This perspective expands our understanding of technological systems by including living beings as active participants, challenging the traditional boundaries between technology, nature, and culture.

Previous studies have explored animals, especially horses, as both workforce and living machines [10,57,59]. This perspective connects animal technologies to broader discussions in environmental and technological history. Technologies shape who we are, and animals have often been studied in three main technical categories: agriculture and food production; energy and transport; and animal-based scientific studies (e.g., biotechnology, ecology, evolutionary biology, and zoology). In Horses at Work [10], Greene shows how studying animal technologies can enrich the field of technology history by linking them to cultural, economic, and military contexts. Just as horses, dogs can be analysed as part of a technological system, whose historical role helped shape human societies. Cultural history helps us understand societies consisting of both humans and animals, living and working together under shared, but unequal, social norms. In the history of technology, which is a dynamic and evolving field, it is important to recognize that animals can be powerful, material, and human-shaped, like machines, but also living, sensing, and conscious beings. This challenges the clear division between human and non-human actors [60].

Dogs are not just biological beings, they are the result of millennia of co-evolution and technological interaction, optimized for specific roles in environments. As humans play an increasingly active role in ecological and evolutionary processes, it becomes more important to recognize living beings as integral parts of technological systems, both as material resources and as co-creators of human experience and culture [61]. Sled dogs are not just working animals; they represent a living cultural heritage and evidence to the long-standing and complex relationship between humans and animals in the Arctic [62]. To understand the continued relevance of sled dogs in technological and cultural systems, we must recognize their role not only as animals but as carriers of knowledge, tradition, and identity. Sled dogs embody intangible cultural heritage, a body of knowledge, stories, sounds, and movements that cannot be learned from books but only through lived experience. This knowledge is passed down through generations, including through the dogs themselves [56,58]. Recognizing sled dogs as intangible heritage is essential to understanding their full significance [62]. It is not only about preserving a tradition, but about maintaining a living relationship between humans, animals, and the landscape, one that includes technical skills, emotional bonds, and legacy.

4.1. Dogs as Part of Technological Systems

The discussion regarding whether animals can be considered technology likely comes from the influence of the Industrial Revolution. This period emphasized machines replacing nature, such as horses being replaced by automobiles, leading to the belief that only non-living machines count as technology. However, throughout history, humans have used many tools, some mechanical, others not, all of which are forms of technology. These tools often come from nature, which humans have optimised for their needs [11,14]. Although many technologies consist of non-living materials, some tools are living organisms. Organisms become tools when they are used to meet human needs or purposes. Most domesticated plants and animals have been transformed and can be considered as human-made objects [13]. Terms like “biotechnology” and “genetic engineering” show how biological and artificial systems combine to create new tools and technology. For around 10,000 years, humans have turned wild species into domesticated ones to support farming. All established societies rely on biotechnology, recognizing this long history helps us understand modern genetic engineering [13]. One way to consider animals as technology is to perceive them as products, used for transport, food, or companionship. Breeding has also aimed to standardize these products; dog breeders are skilled in this, and even people unfamiliar with dogs can often recognize different breeds. The idea of a “pedigree” has become a symbol of quality in dog breeding [63].

Animals have also performed as a workforce. Sometimes they replace or support human workers, like herding dogs helping shepherds, at a lower cost than human labour [64]. In other cases, animals do tasks humans cannot, such as detecting bombs or drugs with their strong sense of smell. Animals have also been used instead of machines [61].

4.2. Sled Dogs as Part of Arctic Technological Systems

For centuries, dogs have been used for transport in the North because they are well adapted to the environment. Arctic communities have also tamed reindeer for milk, pulling loads, and carrying goods [65]. Studies of horses as living machines help us understand sled dogs as technology in Arctic societies [10,57]. Like horses, sled dogs were essential for transport, but they also had social and cultural roles. Their use involved breeding, equipment, and human interaction, showing that animals are not just tools but active parts of technological systems. Research on human–animal relationships and animal technology shows how sled dogs were more than just transport; they were part of a system shaped by social, economic, and environmental factors (Figure 2) [60]. As new technologies entered the Arctic, it became important to understand how they changed human–animal–technology relationships. The shift from dog sleds to snowmobiles shows that modernization is not just about efficiency; it also affects culture and adaptation. Since the mid-20th century, many Inuit and Arctic communities have adopted snowmobiles. Although snowmobiles are fast and can carry heavy loads, they have not fully replaced sled dogs. In fact, across the Arctic both are now used together. Many traditional hunters still see sleds as more reliable and durable [66].

In Greenland, recent studies show that switching from sled dogs to snowmobiles is not just about technology; it also involves identity, tradition, and climate change [16,67]. In Kulusuk, East Greenland, people say snowmobiles changed how they move around, but sled dogs still matter for hunting, tourism, and cultural heritage [67]. Similar trends are seen in Alaska, where motorized transport has deeply affected both the environment and community life. According to Francis [68], this shift has changed the social and economic system, risking the loss of traditional knowledge. In the Canadian Arctic, this has been called the “snowmobile revolution,” where snowmobiles largely replaced sled dogs in the 1960s. This change was driven by practical needs and government modernization efforts, but it also sparked debates about losing cultural continuity and sustainability [64,69].

Due to climate change, changing ways of living, and geopolitical shifts, traditional sled dog practices and their cultural heritage are increasingly at risk. Understanding the long-term relationship between humans and dogs is important not only for learning about past survival strategies but also for preserving the genetic and cultural heritage of these animals [70]. These practices formed complete technological systems, yet sled dogs have often been ignored in studies of 19th- and 20th-century technology, despite their key role in Arctic life. Separating sled dogs from technology is in contrast to how society perceived them within the Arctic. Fascinated by mechanics, people often used technological metaphors to describe and understand sled dogs as sources of power and to find ways to improve their endurance, strength, and efficiency [66]. What is considered technology changes over time. To understand Arctic technology history, we must recognize how past societies understood and used technology, not just as machines and tools, but as living actors in a dynamic relation between humans, animals, and landscape (Figure 2).

5. Conclusions

Technology is not limited to mechanical devices, and many technologies were developed before machines were invented. The domestication and use of animals have played a central role in the development of technological knowledge and practice [12]. Sled dogs are an example of this. Over thousands of years, they have been selectively bred and trained to perform specific tasks in Arctic environments, making them living technologies or biological systems adapted to human needs in the Arctic.

Building on this perspective, we propose the Transportation Hypothesis as a framework for considering whether mobility and transport may have contributed to the development and specialization of the human–dog relationship. Existing models of dog domestication have primarily emphasized commensal scavenging, hunting partnerships, or social companionship as important contexts for the emergence of this relationship. While these explanations are not mutually exclusive, they may not fully account for the technological significance of mobility. The Transportation Hypothesis therefore proposes that, once early wolves became sufficiently tolerant of humans, their capacity to reduce the energetic costs of moving people, camps, and resources may have provided an additional context in which human investment in dogs became advantageous. Importantly, this hypothesis does not establish transportation as the cause or initiating mechanism of dog domestication. Rather, it identifies transportation as a potential technological dimension of the longer process through which human–dog relationships developed and became increasingly specialized.

The primary challenge in the investigation of the origin of the dog is defining the moment when a dog is no longer a wolf and has instead become differentiated enough to be called a ‘dog’. This presents complications in not only determining when and where dogs would have originated but also in determining why they came to be in the first place. As a result, the precise moment will likely never be pinpointed; however, researchers can continue to seek evidence for where the earliest distinct individuals appear and what cultural context they are derived from. Locating evidence for use of dogs as aids in hunting, guarding, and companions before written records will be limited to indirect evidence such as pictorial representations. Future genetic research exploring adaptations in early dogs may uncover evidence for selective breeding for culturally valuable traits outside of those indicating the selection in sled dogs and may provide further insight into alternative explanations for the roles of early dogs.

This perspective reframes domestication as a technological process rather than solely a biological or behavioural one. Selective breeding, training, and the development of transport technologies, including harnesses and sleds, can be understood as components of a longer technological relationship between humans and dogs. The sled should therefore not be regarded as the beginning of transport technology, but as a later development within a broader history in which humans and dogs adapted to one another through shared labour and movement across landscapes. The archaeological and genomic evidence currently available does not establish that transportation initiated dog domestication, but it provides a basis for considering mobility as one possible dimension of the technological relationship between humans and dogs.

Recognising sled dogs as living technologies also highlights their significance as intangible cultural heritage. Their value lies not only in their genetics or working ability but in the accumulated body of ecological knowledge, technical skills, oral traditions, and social practices transmitted through generations of people and dogs together. This relationship is best understood as one of co-domestication, in which humans and dogs have mutually shaped one another biologically, culturally, and technologically. Conserving sled dogs therefore means preserving not only a distinctive animal population but one of humanity’s oldest continuously functioning technological systems and a living partnership through which movement, survival, and culture have co-evolved for millennia.
